Submillimetre hot-electron transport in manganese-doped quantum dot solids

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 47 min read (9326 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~47 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that colloidal quantum dot solids are promising for photoconversion and photochemistry, but their performance is fundamentally limited by rapid hot-carrier cooling, low carrier mobility and short transport ranges1.
  • Photoconversion processes underpin technologies ranging from photodetection and photovoltaics to photoemission and photochemistry.
  • Recent findings suggest that recent studies have shown that hot carriers can be manipulated using ultrafast spin exchange (SE) interactions in manganese (Mn)-doped colloidal quantum dots (QDs)10,11,12.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that colloidal quantum dot solids are promising for photoconversion and photochemistry, but their performance is fundamentally limited by rapid hot-carrier cooling, low carrier mobility and short transport ranges1. Here we demonstrate a spin-exchange-driven phototransport regime in manganese-doped quantum dot films that enables the generation, long-range transport and regeneration of hot carriers. Ultrafast spin-exchange-mediated Auger upconversion promotes electrons into high-energy, delocalized states before phonon cooling2,3, establishing a transient high-mobility conduction channel. Crucially, spin-exchange interactions not only generate hot carriers but also enable their repeated re-excitation, thereby sustaining long-range drift. This mechanism yields room-temperature mobilities of about 150 cm2 V−1 s−1 and submillimetre drift lengths—far greater than those of conventional quantum dot solids and approaching values characteristic of crystalline semiconductors. Time-of-flight measurements confirm drift-dominated transport, with transit times scaling linearly with distance and inversely with electric field. These results establish a route to long-range energy transport in nanoscale materials and enable the use of hot carriers in photoconversion, photochemistry and transit-time-limited photodetection.

Photoconversion processes underpin technologies ranging from photodetection and photovoltaics to photoemission and photochemistry. Their ability to exploit excess photon energy is limited by rapid phonon-assisted cooling of nonequilibrium (‘hot’) carriers to band-edge states, typically within picoseconds, severely restricting their lifetime and transport range. Stabilizing and transporting hot carriers therefore remains a substantial challenge for advanced solar-energy conversion4,5,6,7 and high-energy photochemistry8,9.

Recent findings suggest that recent studies have shown that hot carriers can be manipulated using ultrafast spin exchange (SE) interactions in manganese (Mn)-doped colloidal quantum dots (QDs)10,11,12. These interactions mediate subpicosecond Auger-type energy transfer between QD excitons and Mn spin states, reaching energy-transfer rates of about 10 eV ps−1 (ref. 11), well above typical phonon-related energy-loss rates (≲1 eV ps−1)13,14. By outcompeting intraband cooling, SE-Auger processes provide an efficient pathway for harvesting hot-electron energy, enabling phenomena such as visible-light generation of solvated electrons2,15 and carrier multiplication12.

Sources indicate that here we demonstrate that SE-Auger upconversion in Mn-doped QD films promotes photoelectrons into high-energy, delocalized transport states, enabling rapid, long-range hot-carrier transport through the QD solid. Transient photocurrent (TPC) measurements reveal time-of-flight (ToF) dynamics with drift mobilities of about 150 cm2 V−1 s−1 and submillimetre transport distances—well beyond those typically observed in QD solids. These results establish a route to long-range hot-carrier transport for photoconversion and hot-electron-driven photochemistry.

We prepared undoped (reference) and Mn-doped CdSe QDs overcoated with a thin protective CdS shell (Methods). We focus on CdSe/CdS QDs with an initial core radius of rCdSe ≈ 1.65 nm. The undoped sample exhibits a photoluminescence (PL) peak at about 2.15 eV and a band-edge (1S) absorption feature at about 2.23 eV (Fig. 1a, black curves).

a, Absorption (solid lines) and PL (dashed lines) spectra of undoped (black), lightly doped (blue) and heavily doped (red) QDs. The orange arrow marks the internal Mn spin-flip transition (EMn = 2.1 eV). Insets, schematics of undoped (top), lightly doped (middle) and heavily doped (bottom) CdSe/CdS QDs. In the heavily doped sample, an interfacial MnxCd1−xSe barrier layer forms between the CdSe core and CdS shell. b, PL dynamics of undoped (black), lightly doped (blue) and heavily doped (red) QDs. Single-exponential fits to the undoped and lightly doped traces (dashed lines) yield τPL,0 = 35 ns and τPL,Mn = 61 ns, respectively; a double-exponential fit to the heavily doped trace (dashed red line) gives an average lifetime of ⟨τPL,Mn⟩ = 225 ns. Inset, forward (time constant τF, solid black arrows) and backward (τB, dashed black arrows) SE-driven excitation transfer between the QD exciton and Mn spin excitation. Short red arrows indicate the spin orientation of electrons (filled red circles); for holes (open red circles), the arrow denotes the spin of the electron removed to create the hole. c, Tail-normalized band-edge bleach dynamics of the undoped sample as a function of ⟨N⟩, the average number of excitons generated per QD per pulse; ΔαBE is the pump-induced change in the band-edge absorption coefficient. At ⟨N⟩ ≳ 1, a fast component emerges owing to multiexciton Auger recombination, illustrated in the bottom inset for a biexciton (XX). Top inset, biexciton dynamics obtained by subtracting tail-normalized traces measured at ⟨N⟩ = 1.32 and 0.19 (circles); a single-exponential fit (line) gives τA = 85 ps. d, Corresponding dynamics for lightly doped QDs show strongly accelerated decay owing to SE-Auger recombination (note the 8-ps time window compared with 800 ps in c). The SE-Auger lifetimes of hybrid biexciton (X–Mn*) and triexciton (XX–Mn*) states, extracted using the subtraction procedure (top inset), are τSE-A = 0.91 ps and 0.23 ps, respectively. The SE-Auger process is illustrated in the bottom inset. All measurements were performed on QD solutions in toluene; time-resolved PL and TA measurements used 150-fs, 2.4-eV excitation pulses. a.u., arbitrary units.

According to recent reports, mn-doped samples were synthesized by diffusion doping of the CdSe cores, involving partial Cd2+ → Mn2+ cation exchange near the surface followed by Mn diffusion into the core interior16,17 (Methods). The Mn content was controlled by the doping time (tMn = 5–30 min). Here we examine samples prepared with tMn = 10 and 20 min, referred to as ‘lightly’ and ‘heavily’ doped QDs, respectively.

Sources indicate that the lightly doped QDs show spectral features similar to those of the undoped reference (Fig. 1a, blue curves), indicating no appreciable change in the effective CdSe core size. The heavily doped sample exhibits an approximately 130-meV blue shift of both PL and absorption (Fig. 1a, red curves), consistent with a reduction of the effective CdSe core radius to about 1.35 nm owing to formation of a higher-bandgap MnxCd1−xSe surface layer.

Mn incorporation strongly modifies single-exciton PL dynamics measured at low excitation levels (⟨N⟩ < 0.1, in which ⟨N⟩ is the average number of excitons generated per QD per pulse). The PL lifetime increases from τPL,0 = 35 ns in undoped QDs to τPL,Mn = 61 ns in lightly doped QDs and to an average of 225 ns in heavily doped QDs (Fig. 1b).

This behaviour arises from ultrafast (subpicosecond) bidirectional SE-mediated excitation transfer between the QD exciton (X) and the internal Mn spin-flip transition (EMn = 2.1 eV)2,10,18. In the forward process, the QD exciton relaxes while promoting the Mn ion from the spin-up 6A1 ground state to the spin-down 4T1 state (Fig. 1b, inset). This occurs through two concerted spin-conserving transfers: a spin-up Mn 3d electron fills the QD valence-band (VB) hole, while a spin-down QD conduction-band (CB) electron is simultaneously transferred into the Mn 3d shell. In the reverse process, spin-flip relaxation of the excited Mn ion (Mn*) regenerates a QD exciton.

In a recent development, the rapid forward and backward transfers establish a quasi-steady-state distribution between excitonic and Mn-based states, with occupation probabilities pX and pMn related by pX/pMn = exp[−(ΕX − ΕMn)/δ0], in which ΕX is the exciton energy (determined from the PL peak energy) and δ0 = 103 meV is an experimentally determined characteristic energy3,11. Because the intrinsic Mn* lifetime is very long (τMn ≳ 1 ms; ref. 18), decay of the coupled X–Mn system is governed by its excitonic component, 1/τPL,Mn ≈ pX/τPL,0.

In a recent development, for the lightly doped sample, in which EMn ≈ EX, pX ≈ pMn, giving τPL,Mn ≈ 2τPL,0 ≈ 70 ns, close to the measured 61 ns. For the heavily doped sample (ΕX − ΕMn = 188 meV), the model yields τPL,Mn ≈ 7.2τPL,0 ≈ 252 ns, again close to the observed 225 ns. The prolonged lifetime of the coupled X–Mn excitation facilitates multiexciton formation and thereby supports the SE-Auger processes underlying the long-range hot-electron transport discussed below.

Although slowing single-exciton decay, Mn doping greatly accelerates multiexciton dynamics, which in undoped QDs are governed by Auger recombination, for which electron–hole recombination energy is transferred to a third carrier within the same QD19 (Fig. 1c, bottom inset). In the undoped sample, this process appears as a fast decay component in transient absorption (TA) traces (Methods), emerging near ⟨N⟩ ≈ 1 (Fig. 1c). From this component, we extract a biexciton Auger lifetime of τA = 85 ps (Fig. 1c, top inset).

Recent findings suggest that in Mn-doped QDs, the TA decay also accelerates near ⟨N⟩ ≈ 1 (Fig. 1d, lightly doped sample), but the corresponding time constant is nearly two orders of magnitude shorter, about 910 fs, and decreases further to about 230 fs at higher excitation levels (Fig. 1d, top inset). These subpicosecond dynamics arise from SE-Auger recombination of hybrid multiexciton states comprising intrinsic QD excitons and excited Mn ions2,3. In the electron re-excitation pathway (Fig. 1d, bottom inset), two concerted spin-transfer events promote a spin-down Mn 3d electron into a hot QD CB state, whereas the Mn ion is restored to its ground-state configuration by transfer of a spin-up electron from the QD band-edge CB state. As a result, the hot electron is elevated above the QD band edge by EMn.

Previous studies established that the SE-Auger rate depends mainly on exciton multiplicity and only weakly on the number of excited Mn ions3. Accordingly, the observed time constants of 910 and 230 fs are consistent with SE-Auger decay of hybrid biexciton (X–Mn*) and triexciton (XX–Mn*) states, respectively3.

It has been revealed that A key consequence is the very high energy-gain rate associated with SE-Auger upconversion (rgain). For τSE-A = 230 fs, rgain = rSE-A = EMn/τSE-A ≈ 9 eV ps−1, far exceeding typical phonon-assisted energy-loss rates (rphon ≲ 1 eV ps−1)13,14. Thus, SE-Auger upconversion can outcompete phonon cooling and efficiently generate and manipulate hot carriers.

Industry observers note that A high SE-Auger upconversion rate could enable Auger-assisted hot-carrier transport with strongly enhanced photoconductance. Specifically, theory predicts that Auger excitation above the QD ionization threshold can promote electrons into delocalized, ‘quasi-free’ states with greatly increased mobility20. Experimentally, short-lived bursts of enhanced carrier mobility were previously observed in undoped PbSe QD films21 and attributed to Auger-generated hot electrons that remained confined within individual QDs. The corresponding transport range was, however, limited to the approximately 50–100-nm near-contact region. Here we use ultrafast SE-Auger interactions to promote electrons above the confinement barrier, as originally foreseen in ref. 20, and show that this enables submillimetre transport.

Sources indicate that the concept of Auger-enhanced conductivity is illustrated in Fig. 2a. If an electron is excited above the QD confinement barrier—that is, effectively ejected from the QD—it can access a high-mobility transport band formed by closely spaced, delocalized peripheral states22. In typical CdSe QDs, however, direct ejection of a band-edge electron by a single conventional Auger upconversion step is unfavourable because the transferred energy, approximately equal to the bandgap Eg, is smaller than the confinement barrier. Ejection can still occur from higher-lying transient states (Fig. 2a) but rapid phonon cooling usually returns carriers to the band edge before Auger upconversion can take place.

a, Schematic of Auger-assisted hot-carrier photoconductance. Absorption of an above-band-edge photon (wavy blue arrow) in a QD containing a pre-existing electron generates a multicarrier (trion) state that undergoes Auger recombination, promoting an electron into a high-energy, delocalized hot state. Access to this state requires retention of the photogenerated electron’s excess energy and is therefore efficient only when the Auger energy-transfer rate (rA) exceeds the phonon-assisted energy-loss rate (rphon). b, Schematic of the Auston switch device containing a QD film as the photoactive layer (top) and the experimental geometry (bottom). The QD film within the 70-µm gap (L) between two gold (Au) electrodes is excited by a focused laser beam whose position can be translated across the gap; d denotes the distance between the beam centre and the positive electrode. c, Photocurrent transients for the undoped sample as a function of excitation level (⟨N⟩ = 0.23–5.38). Inset, tail-normalized TPC traces for ⟨N⟩ = 0.23 and 2.00 (black); their difference (red) is fitted to a single exponential, yielding a biexciton Auger lifetime of τA = 110 ps. Measurements used 150-fs, 3.6-eV excitation pulses with the beam centred at d = 15 μm. IRF denotes the instrument response function. d, TPC traces for the heavily doped sample under identical conditions exhibit markedly different behaviour at high ⟨N⟩, developing a pronounced step-like component whose amplitude increases rapidly—approximately cubically—with ⟨N⟩ (inset). a.u., arbitrary units.

Sources indicate that owing to its ultrafast character, SE-Auger upconversion can overcome this limitation by ejecting a nonthermalized electron before it loses its excess energy to phonons11. Band-edge electrons can also be expelled from the QD through two sequential SE-Auger upconversion steps2.

According to recent reports, to investigate the role of SE interactions in phototransport, we performed TPC measurements using Auston switch devices in which undoped or Mn-doped QD films were incorporated into a 70-µm gap of a 50-Ω microstrip transmission line21,23,24,25 (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 1; Methods). The QDs were excited by 150-fs laser pulses focused into a narrow stripe (70–80 µm full width at half maximum, FWHM), whose position within the gap was varied by translating the sample. The TPC signal was recorded with a 20-GHz sampling oscilloscope, yielding an overall temporal resolution of approximately 50 ps.

Dark-conductivity measurements (Extended Data Fig. 2) show that the QD films are highly resistive at equilibrium, indicating that the TPC response is dominated by photogenerated rather than equilibrium carriers.

In most experiments, the QDs were excited at Ephot = 3.6 eV, more than 1 eV above the band edge. Under these conditions, SE-Auger interactions can efficiently eject electrons from Mn-doped QDs11, whereas ejection by means of slower conventional Auger processes in undoped QDs is much less likely. Thus, any strong enhancement of photoconductance provides a direct signature of SE-Auger-driven hot-carrier generation and transport.

In Fig. 2c,d, we compare pump-intensity-dependent photocurrent transients for undoped and Mn-doped QD films, respectively, measured at a device bias of V = 100 V and Ephot = 3.6 eV.

For the undoped sample, the excitation range corresponds to ⟨N⟩ from 0.23 to 5.38 excitons per QD. Increasing pump fluence does not substantially alter the overall TPC profile; the main effect is an acceleration of the early-time decay at ⟨N⟩ ≳ 1, similar to the behaviour observed in TA measurements (Fig. 1c) and likewise indicative of multiexciton Auger recombination. A biexciton Auger lifetime extracted from the fast TPC component (about 110 ps; Fig. 2c, inset) agrees reasonably well with that obtained from TA (about 85 ps; Fig. 1c, inset).

In a recent development, the ⟨N⟩ dependence of both the early-time TPC peak amplitude (time t = tpeak) and the long-time signal (t = 400 ps > τA) is also well described by the Auger recombination model (Fig. 3a, black symbols and lines). In this model, the peak photocurrent contains contributions from both single-exciton and multiexciton states, whereas after Auger decay, the long-time signal originates only from single excitons (Supplementary Note 1).

Recent findings suggest that a, Early-time peak TPC signal (open squares) and long-time (t = 400 ps; post-Auger decay) TPC amplitude (filled black circles) for the undoped sample as a function of ⟨N⟩, extracted from Fig. 2c. The data are described by a model assuming Poisson-distributed initial exciton occupancies and constant carrier mobility (black lines). For the doped sample, the TPC step amplitude at t = 400 ps (filled red circles; from Fig. 2d) increases rapidly for ⟨N⟩ > 1, indicating a strong increase in carrier mobility. The data are reproduced by a model of SE-Auger-assisted activation into a high-mobility hot-electron transport band (red line). b, Schematic of SE-Auger upconversion involving an electron in a transient above-band-edge state. This process competes with phonon-assisted relaxation (‘cooling’) at rate rphon. Efficient promotion of electrons into the hot-carrier transport band requires the SE-Auger energy-transfer rate rSE-A to exceed rphon. c, Early-time TA spectra of a heavily doped QD film (Ephot = 3.6 eV, Δt = 3 ps) for ⟨N⟩ ≲ 1 (green and blue) and ⟨N⟩ ≳ 1 (red and black). Below the SE-Auger onset, the spectra are dominated by the band-edge bleach from state filling. Above the onset, a pronounced photoinduced absorption develops below the bleach, producing the derivative-like lineshape characteristic of a carrier-induced Stark effect. Inset, SE-Auger activation into a delocalized transport state spatially separates the electron and hole wavefunctions, generating a local electric field (Feh, red arrow) that shifts the band-edge transition by ΔESt. a.u., arbitrary units.

According to recent reports, these results show that TPC dynamics in undoped QD films are dominated by carrier recombination, with no detectable signatures of transit across the electrode gap. The corresponding transit times are therefore much longer than the characteristic recombination times because of the low carrier mobility.

In contrast to the undoped samples, photocurrent transients from Mn-doped QD films change markedly with increasing pump fluence (Fig. 2d, heavily doped sample). At ⟨N⟩ ≳ 1, the TPC traces develop a pronounced step-like component whose amplitude grows approximately cubically with ⟨N⟩ (IPC,400ps ∝ ⟨N⟩3.05; Fig. 2d, inset), where IPC,400ps is the photocurrent amplitude measured at t = 400 ps after excitation. This superlinear growth cannot be explained by the increase in carrier population alone and instead indicates an increase in carrier mobility by orders of magnitude.

The onset of this rapid photocurrent growth coincides with the threshold for SE-Auger recombination, suggesting SE-Auger-driven activation of electrons into a higher-energy transport band above the QD confinement barrier, as proposed in ref. 20. The absence of this effect in undoped QDs further points to the critical role of ultrafast SE-Auger upconversion, which can intercept an energetic photoelectron before intraband cooling and promote it into a peripheral, delocalized state outside the QD (Fig. 3b).

It has been revealed that the excitation-level dependence of the TPC step amplitude (evaluated at t = 400 ps) further supports its SE-Auger origin. As detailed in Supplementary Note 2, the data are well described using the previously established (n − 1)2 scaling of the SE-Auger rate with exciton multiplicity n (Fig. 3a, red symbols and line)3.

In a recent development, further evidence for electron ejection from the QD is provided by pump-fluence-dependent TA spectra (Fig. 3c). At ⟨N⟩ < 1, the spectra are dominated by a state-filling bleach at 2.34 eV, whereas at ⟨N⟩ ≳ 1, they evolve into a derivative-like lineshape characteristic of electron ejection11,26. The resulting spatial separation of the ejected electron and the hole remaining in the QD generates an internal electric field (Fig. 3c, inset) that redshifts the band-edge transition through the Stark effect, producing induced absorption below the original bleach.

Sources indicate that A step-like TPC signal with an abrupt cut-off is a hallmark of ToF photocurrent observed in high-mobility photoconductors, in which photocarriers are rapidly swept from the photoconductive gap by drift towards the electrodes27,28,29. In this regime, the photocurrent duration is determined not by carrier relaxation but by the carrier transit time, ttr = d/vd = d/(μF), in which d is the transport distance, vd the drift velocity, μ the carrier mobility and F the electric field.

To test for ToF transport in Mn-doped QD films, we measured photocurrent transients as a function of both transport distance and electric field, F = V/L, in which L = 70 μm is the electrode gap. Figure 4a highlights TPC traces for heavily doped QDs at three distances from the positive electrode, d = 15, 45 and 65 µm. The TPC pulse duration increases systematically with d, a defining signature of carrier transit27 and evidence that the photoresponse is dominated by high-mobility hot electrons generated by SE-Auger upconversion2,30,31.

Sources indicate that a, TPC traces for heavily doped QDs measured at V = 100 V, Ephot = 3.6 eV and ⟨N⟩ = 5.12 (solid lines) for d = 15 µm (red), 45 µm (blue) and 65 µm (green). Dashed lines are fits to the ToF model, yielding vd = 24 µm ns−1, 22 µm ns−1 and 13 µm ns−1, respectively, with τ0 = 7 ns. Inset, transit time as a function of d, determined from the inflection points of log–log TPC plots (symbols) for V = 100 V (red) and 70 V (black). Linear fits (lines) yield vd = 21.5 ± 0.4 µm ns−1 and 15.3 ± 0.4 µm ns−1, respectively. b, Model of hot-electron transport with SE-Auger generation and regeneration. SE-Auger recombination of a hybrid biexciton promotes an electron into a high-mobility transport band above the QD confinement barrier. During drift, the hot electron may partially relax into internal QD states, from which it can be re-excited into the transport band by SE-Auger energy transfer from a long-lived excited Mn ion, sustaining long-range transport. a.u., arbitrary units.

The complementary holes remain largely confined within the CdSe cores and are not expected to contribute appreciably to the fast TPC response. However, we do not detect persistent charge accumulation in the photoconductive gap, probably because the non-zero dark conductivity of the QD films (Extended Data Fig. 2) enables charge neutralization between successive excitation pulses.

In a recent development, the measured TPC profiles are well described by the error-function form of the ToF expression for a Gaussian photoexcitation profile (dashed lines in Fig. 4a; Supplementary Note 3 and Extended Data Fig. 3). Minor deviations include an initial capacitive spike29,32 and a weak long-time tail associated with delayed electrons, discussed below.

Modelling of the d = 15 μm trace yields a drift velocity of vd = 24 μm ns−1 and an effective lifetime τ0 = 7 ns. In conventional ToF models, τ0 describes recombination and/or trapping of mobile carriers. Here it instead represents the effective lifetime of the high-mobility hot-electron population. Whereas hot electrons normally cool to the band edge within a few picoseconds14,33, in Mn-doped QDs, their lifetime is extended by SE-Auger regeneration (Fig. 4b). Long-lived Mn excitations persist during carrier transit and can repeatedly re-excite partially relaxed electrons into the transport band before complete cooling. Regeneration is imperfect, however: if a relaxing electron encounters a QD lacking an excited Mn ion or otherwise unable to support SE-Auger re-excitation, it relaxes into a low-mobility band-edge state. Thus, τ0 represents the average survival time of the regenerated hot-electron population.

It has been revealed that toF fits at longer transport distances yield an apparent decrease in vd from 24 μm ns−1 at d = 15 μm to 13 μm ns−1 at d = 65 μm, whereas τ0 remains essentially unchanged (Fig. 4a). We attribute this reduction to the increasing contribution of delayed electrons that progressively lose mobility as regeneration becomes less effective, broadening the trailing edge of the TPC transient. The shortest-distance value, vd = 24 μm ns−1, therefore provides the best estimate of the intrinsic drift velocity of the regenerated hot-electron population.

According to recent reports, we also estimate the transit time with the commonly used empirical approach, in which ttr is identified from the inflection point of a log–log TPC plot, determined from the intersection of power-law fits to the pre-transit and post-transit regions27,28,34,35 (Fig. 5a). The resulting ttr values scale linearly with d (Fig. 4a, inset), as expected for ToF transport. The slope yields vd = 21.5 ± 0.4 µm ns−1, in good agreement with the value obtained from error-function modelling of the d = 15 μm trace (vd = 24 µm ns−1).

At a lower bias (V = 70 V), ttr again scales linearly with d (Fig. 4a, inset and Extended Data Fig. 4), yielding vd = 15.3 ± 0.4 µm ns−1. The ratio of drift velocities at 70 V and 100 V (0.71) closely matches the voltage ratio (0.7), confirming the expected linear dependence of vd on electric field. Bias-dependent measurements at fixed distances (d = 45 µm and 25 µm; Fig. 5b and Extended Data Fig. 5) provide an independent test: ttr increases with decreasing bias following the expected 1/V dependence (Fig. 5c).

Industry observers note that a, Log–log plot of distance-dependent TPC traces measured for a heavily doped QD film at V = 100 V under 3.6-eV excitation with ⟨N⟩ = 5.12. The traces are vertically offset for clarity. Straight dashed lines show power-law fits to the pre-transit and post-transit regions of the uppermost TPC trace. Their intersection defines the carrier transit time ttr (red diamonds). b, Bias-dependent TPC traces measured at d = 45 µm under the same excitation conditions. Carrier transit times determined from the inflection points of the log–log traces are indicated by red diamonds. c, Transit time ttr versus bias V for d = 45 µm (open black squares) and 25 µm (filled red circles). Fits to ttr = (1/µe)(dL/V) yield electron mobilities of µe = 144 cm2 V−1 s−1 and 156 cm2 V−1 s−1, respectively. d, Transit time versus d/F combining distance-dependent (green and red symbols) and bias-dependent (black and blue symbols) measurements. The d/F axis is multiplied by 10 so that, with ttr in ns and d/F in µm2 V−1, the slope directly equals 1/µe for µe expressed in cm2 V−1 s−1. The data follow the expected linear dependence for ToF transport (line), yielding an average electron drift mobility of ⟨µe⟩ = 150 ± 11 cm2 V−1 s−1. The shaded region represents the one-standard-error uncertainty of the fitted mobility. a.u., arbitrary units.

Figure 5d summarizes all distance-dependent and bias-dependent measurements (25 data points) by plotting ttr versus d/F, with the horizontal axis scaled by a factor of 10 for convenient unit conversion, as described in the figure caption. For ToF transport, ttr = d/vd = (1/µ)(d/F), so the data should follow a straight line with slope 1/µ. The experimental data indeed collapse onto a single linear trend (Fig. 5d, black line), yielding an average electron mobility of ⟨µe⟩ = 150 ± 11 cm2 V−1 s−1, consistent with values obtained independently from the distance-dependent and bias-dependent data (Fig. 4a, inset and Fig. 5c).

The ToF behaviour is reproducible across independently synthesized QD batches and several Auston switch devices. Further measurements yield electron mobilities of around 150–170 cm2 V−1 s−1 (Extended Data Fig. 6), confirming the robustness of the high-mobility hot-electron transport regime.

According to recent reports, although the present study focuses on 3.6-eV excitation, long-range hot-electron transport is also observed under near-band-edge excitation at 2.4 eV (Extended Data Fig. 7). In this case, the onset of the rapid TPC increase shifts from ⟨N⟩ ≈ 1 to ⟨N⟩ ≈ 2, consistent with the SE-Auger ionization model. Because ejection of a near-band-edge electron requires two sequential SE-Auger upconversion steps, ionization occurs only once three excitons are generated, in agreement with previous observations of SE-driven photoionization2. Above this threshold, the transport characteristics are essentially unchanged: bias-dependent and distance-dependent TPC measurements exhibit the same ToF behaviour and yield ⟨μe⟩ = 164 cm2 V−1 s−1, close to the value obtained under 3.6-eV excitation.

It has been revealed that the measured drift mobility, ⟨μe⟩ ≈ 150 cm2 V−1 s−1, is about an order of magnitude higher than values typically reported for strongly coupled, device-grade QD films (10–20 cm2 V−1 s−1) (refs. 1,36) and approaches the room-temperature electron drift mobilities of bulk wide-bandgap II–VI semiconductors (approximately 200–600 cm2 V−1 s−1) (ref. 37). This comparison serves only as a benchmark of mobility magnitude and does not imply equivalent transport mechanisms or device operation.

In a recent development, the high hot-electron mobility also enables long transport distances. Using τ0 = 7 ns and vd = 21.5 µm ns−1 (V = 100 V) gives a drift range of about 0.15 mm. Such transport distances are extraordinary for colloidal QD solids and place Mn-doped QD films in a transport regime more commonly associated with crystalline semiconductors than with ligand-linked nanocrystal assemblies. Collectively, these results demonstrate a high-mobility transport regime in which SE-Auger excitation promotes photoelectrons into a delocalized hot-carrier transport band, whereas repeated SE-Auger regeneration sustains their long-range drift (Fig. 4b).

We report a phototransport regime in which SE-Auger upconversion dynamically promotes electrons into a delocalized, high-mobility band above the QD confinement barrier, yielding carrier mobilities of about 150 cm2 V−1 s−1 and submillimetre transport distances. Unlike conventional band-like transport, this mechanism does not rely on miniband formation or strong electronic coupling between neighbouring QDs. Instead, repeated SE-Auger activation regenerates high-energy transport states following partial relaxation, sustaining hot-electron transport over nanosecond timescales.

According to recent reports, long-range hot-electron transport can enable transit-time-limited photodetection in the GHz regime, ultrafast optical-to-electrical signal conversion and modulation and electrical sampling of ultrafast optical signals. Beyond optoelectronics, SE-enabled stabilization and transport of hot carriers offer a strategy for harnessing high-energy electrons in photochemical processes. Their high mobility, expanded wavefunctions and strong reducing power make them attractive as both energetic charge carriers and agents of remote chemical transformations.

Cadmium oxide (CdO, 99.99%, Aldrich), octadecylphosphonic acid (ODPA, 99%, PCI), trioctylphosphine oxide (TOPO, 99%, Aldrich), trioctylphosphine (TOP, 97%, Aldrich), diphenylphosphine (DPP, 98%, Aldrich), selenium (Se, 200 mesh, 99.999%, Alfa Aesar), 1-octadecene (ODE, 90%, Aldrich), oleic acid (OA, 90%, Aldrich), oleylamine (OAm, 70%, Aldrich), manganese(II) acetate tetrahydrate (Mn(ac)2·4H2O, 99.999%, Strem) and tributylphosphine (TBP, 95%, Aldrich) were used as received.

Sources indicate that cdSe core particles with a wurtzite crystal structure were synthesized following a previously reported method17. Specifically, 100 mg of CdO, 490 mg of ODPA and 5 g of TOPO were loaded into a three-neck flask and degassed under vacuum at 150 °C for 1 h. Under nitrogen flow, the mixture was heated to 320 °C and maintained at this temperature until it formed a clear solution. Subsequently, 1 ml of TOP was swiftly injected into the flask. After the temperature increased to 380 °C, 1 ml of a 1.4 M TOP–Se solution was rapidly injected. At this stage, 1 mol% of DPP was added to the TOP–Se solution to control the growth kinetics17. After 3 min, the reaction mixture was cooled to room temperature by removing the heating mantle.

The resulting nanocrystals were collected by adding ethanol followed by centrifugation at 8,000 rpm. This washing procedure was repeated three times. The purified nanocrystals were then redispersed in toluene.

In a recent development, to incorporate Mn into the synthesized CdSe nanocrystals, we used a diffusion-doping procedure16 following a refined protocol of ref. 17. To remove residual Cd species, the pre-synthesized CdSe nanocrystals dispersed in toluene were precipitated with ethanol. 75 mg of the precipitate was dissolved in a mixture of 27 ml of degassed ODE and 2.7 ml of OA. The mixture was heated to 60 °C under vacuum for 1 h. After cooling to room temperature, the nanocrystals were again precipitated with ethanol and collected by centrifugation at 8,000 rpm. The resulting precipitate was added to a mixture of 510 mg of Se, 3 ml of degassed ODE and 3 ml of TBP.

Separately, 90 mg of Mn(ac)2·4H2O, 45 ml of ODE, 1.8 ml of OA and 3.9 ml of OAm were loaded into a flask and degassed under vacuum at 100 °C for 1 h. Under nitrogen flow, the mixture was heated to 300 °C, after which the previously prepared CdSe nanocrystal/TBP–Se solution in ODE was swiftly injected. The reaction temperature was maintained at 300 °C and the doping level was controlled by the reaction time (typically 5–30 min). After completion of the reaction, the mixture was cooled to room temperature. Magnetic circular dichroism measurements indicated approximately 2–5 internal Mn2+ dopants per QD, depending on the doping time17.

In a recent development, owing to the large abundance of surface trap states, as-prepared Mn-doped CdSe cores do not exhibit detectable PL. To suppress surface defects, the cores were coated with a CdS shell following procedures reported in ref. 17.

Sources indicate that to prepare a Cd-oleate precursor solution, 123 mg of CdO, 2.45 ml of OA and 10.8 ml of ODE were loaded into a flask and degassed at 100 °C under vacuum for 1 h. Under nitrogen flow, the temperature was increased to 250 °C and maintained for 1 h until a clear solution formed. The precursor solution was then cooled to 100 °C and maintained at this temperature until injection during CdS shell growth.

A TOP–S precursor solution was prepared by stirring a mixture of 18 ml of TOP and 44.3 mg of sulfur powder overnight in a glovebox.

In a recent development, for shell growth, 75 mg of Mn-doped CdSe QDs were dissolved in a mixture of 28 ml of ODE, 2.4 ml of OAm and 1.2 ml of OA. This mixture was degassed at 100 °C under vacuum for 1 h. Under nitrogen flow, the flask was heated to 220 °C and 0.4-ml aliquots of the Cd-oleate and TOP–S precursor solutions were alternately injected dropwise at intervals of 2.5 min for two cycles.

According to recent reports, A 100-nm gold layer was evaporated onto the backside of a 1-mm glass substrate to serve as the ground plane. An approximately 200-nm-thick film of undoped (reference) or Mn-doped CdSe/CdS QDs was then deposited on the top surface of the substrate through repeated spin-coating cycles, accompanied by ligand exchange and rinsing steps. During deposition, QDs dispersed in octane (20 mg ml−1) were spin-coated at 1,600 rpm for 30 s.

In a recent development, to facilitate interdot charge transport, the QDs were cross-linked by means of solid-state ligand exchange, replacing the original long-chain ligands with short bifunctional 1,2-ethanedithiol (EDT) molecules. For ligand exchange, 60 µl of a 1 M EDT solution in methanol (MeOH) was dropped onto the QD layer, allowed to soak for 60 s and then spin-coated at 1,200 rpm for 30 s.

It has been revealed that the film was subsequently rinsed by spin-coating pure MeOH to remove excess ligands. These three steps—QD deposition, ligand exchange and rinsing—were repeated five times to obtain a QD layer approximately 200 nm thick. The resulting film was annealed at 150 °C for 30 min.

Finally, two 200-nm-thick gold contacts separated by a 70-µm gap were deposited on top of the QD film through a shadow mask. Together with the gold ground plane on the backside of the substrate, these contacts form a microstrip transmission line with a nominal impedance of 50 Ω.

To verify that ligand exchange and film fabrication preserved the quantum-confined electronic structure of the QDs, we performed further TA measurements on 200-nm-thick Mn-doped CdSe/CdS QD films prepared using the same ligand-exchange procedure as used for the TPC devices. The TA spectra of the film samples were compared with those of the corresponding QDs in solution under identical excitation conditions (3.6-eV, 150-fs excitation; ⟨N⟩ = 0.3). The results are presented in Extended Data Fig. 8.

To characterize the equilibrium electrical properties of the ligand-exchanged QD films, further dark-conductivity measurements were performed using 120-nm-thick Mn-doped CdSe/CdS QD films deposited on glass substrates and contacted by thermally evaporated interdigitated Au electrodes comprising 25 pairs of 2-mm-long fingers separated by 10 μm. The corresponding current–voltage characteristics are presented in Extended Data Fig. 2.

Sources indicate that electrostatic simulations of the Auston switch geometry were performed using the Electrostatics interface of COMSOL Multiphysics to calculate the electric-field distribution, effective gap capacitance and effective RC constant (Extended Data Fig. 1).

Industry observers note that TA measurements were performed using a standard pump–probe set-up in which absorption changes induced by a short pump pulse were probed in both the temporal and spectral domains using variably delayed probe pulses. The TA system was built around a regeneratively amplified ytterbium-doped potassium gadolinium tungstate (Yb:KGW) femtosecond laser (PHAROS, Light Conversion) generating approximately 190-fs pulses at 1.2 eV.

The laser output was split into two beams. One beam seeded a harmonic generator (HIRO HHG, Light Conversion) to produce second (2.4-eV) or third (3.6-eV) harmonic pump pulses, whose duration was shortened to about 150 fs owing to nonlinear optical pulse compression. Pulses from the second beam were delayed relative to the pump using an optical delay line (up to 5 ns) and focused onto a 3-mm-thick sapphire plate to generate broadband probe pulses in the form of a femtosecond white-light continuum.

It has been revealed that the pump beam was focused onto the sample into a spot with a diameter of about 120 µm, whereas the smaller-diameter probe beam (<90 µm) was centred near the middle of the pump spot. Probe pulses transmitted through the sample were detected using an Avantes AvaSpec-Fast ULS1350F-USB2 spectrometer. The measured TA spectra were corrected for chirp (spectrally dependent delay within the white-light continuum probe pulses) using the procedure described in ref. 2.

In Auger recombination studies of undoped and Mn-doped QDs, we monitored the pump-induced band-edge absorption bleach (ΔαBE), which tracks the decay of band-edge excitonic populations14.

To minimize sample degradation during TPC measurements, the fabricated Auston switch devices were mounted in a nitrogen-filled, airtight chamber equipped with optical windows and electrical feedthroughs. Under these conditions, no measurable changes in the TPC response were observed during the complete characterization of a device, including pump-fluence-dependent, transport-distance-dependent and bias-dependent measurements.

Recent findings suggest that the chamber was mounted on a translation stage, allowing the laser beam position within the electrode gap to be varied. One of the top gold electrodes was biased using a DC power supply (Keithley 2430), whereas the other electrode was connected to a 20-GHz-bandwidth sampling oscilloscope by means of a coaxial cable. To minimize timing jitter, the oscilloscope was triggered by electrical pulses generated by a high-speed Si photodetector driven by a portion of the laser beam split from the excitation path.

According to recent reports, the QDs within the photoconductive gap of the Auston switch were excited at 2.4 eV or 3.6 eV using 150-fs pulses of the second or third harmonic of an amplified Yb:KGW femtosecond PHAROS laser, respectively. The laser beam was focused with a cylindrical achromatic lens into a narrow stripe aligned with the edges of the top gold electrodes. The spatial profile of the excitation beam was approximately Gaussian, with a stripe width of about 70–80 µm (FWHM), measured with a beam profiler. The excitation position within the photoconductive gap of the Auston switch was varied by translating the sample in a plane perpendicular to the laser beam. The position was initially calibrated using a beam profiler and monitored in real time on the sample with a CMOS camera.

According to recent reports, as discussed in Supplementary Note 3, the nonlinear dependence of SE-Auger upconversion on excitation density narrows the lateral spatial profile of the mobile hot-electron population relative to the laser beam profile (Extended Data Fig. 9). Across the film thickness, the initial hot-electron population is weighted towards the illuminated surface. However, because the optical absorption length is comparable with the QD film thickness, excited Mn ions are generated throughout the layer. Consequently, SE-Auger regeneration remains active across the film thickness, even if the hot-electron population spreads vertically during transit within the photoconductive gap.

Sources indicate that a, Top view of the modelled structure consisting of a 200-nm-thick Mn-doped QD film deposited on a 1-mm-thick glass substrate with two 2-mm-wide and 200-nm-thick gold (Au) electrodes separated by a 70-μm gap. The static dielectric constants of the QD film and glass substrate were taken as 6.0 and 4.1, respectively. b, Cross-sectional view showing the calculated electrostatic potential (colour map) and electric-field lines for an applied bias of V = 100 V, obtained using the Electrostatics module of COMSOL Multiphysics. c,d, Calculated horizontal (Ex) and vertical (Ez) electric-field components in the QD film as a function of the distance from the positive electrode. The vertical electric field is negligible over nearly the entire photoconductive gap and becomes appreciable only within approximately 1 μm of the electrode edges. By contrast, the horizontal electric field remains nearly uniform across the gap, with an average value within 10–15% of the nominal field F = V/L. These calculations confirm that the electric field is predominantly horizontal, thereby validating the one-dimensional drift approximation used in the charge transport analysis. The computed electrostatic field distribution yields an effective gap capacitance of approximately 0.2 pF, corresponding to an estimated RC time constant of 10 ps for a 50-Ω transmission line. This value is shorter than the experimental temporal resolution of the TPC measurements (about 50 ps), indicating that the measured response is limited not by the device RC constant but by other components of the measurement circuit and the oscilloscope.

It has been revealed that the measurements were performed on a 120-nm-thick Mn-doped CdSe/CdS QD film deposited on a glass substrate and contacted by thermally evaporated interdigitated Au electrodes comprising 25 pairs of 2-mm-long fingers separated by 10 μm. The measured current exhibits a linear dependence on the applied bias over the investigated voltage range (±60 V), corresponding to maximum electric fields of approximately 6 V μm−1, about four times larger than those used in the TPC experiments. The absence of measurable nonlinearity indicates no detectable contact-limited (Schottky) behaviour under these conditions. The extracted film resistivity is approximately 2.2 × 1010 Ω cm, demonstrating that the ligand-exchanged QD films are highly insulating at equilibrium and therefore contain only a negligible concentration of free carriers.

For a non-zero drift velocity (bottom inset), the transient develops a cut-off when the carrier packet reaches the collecting electrode (the positive contact in the present case, assuming electron-dominated photocurrent). Blue and red traces correspond to vd = 10 µm ns−1 and d = 45 µm (blue line), vd = 20 µm ns−1 and d = 45 µm (solid red line) and vd = 20 µm ns−1 and d = 25 µm (dashed red line). Here d is the distance from the centre of the initial carrier distribution to the charge-collecting electrode and vd is the drift velocity. a.u., arbitrary units.

The measured transit time increases with decreasing V, again consistent with ToF transport. c, Transit time plotted as a function of 10d/F, in which F is the applied electric field, using the data from panels a (blue diamonds) and b (red circles). The factor of 10 is introduced for convenient conversion of the fitted slope to mobility in cm2 V−1 s−1, as described in Fig. 5d. The linear fit (dashed line) yields an average electron mobility of ⟨μe⟩ = 170.6 cm2 V−1 s−1, consistent with the value reported in the main text (Fig. 5d). a.u., arbitrary units.

a, Early-time TPC amplitude as a function of the average number of excitons per QD, ⟨N⟩, measured using 2.4-eV, 150-fs excitation pulses (black squares). For comparison, corresponding data obtained with 3.6-eV excitation are shown by red circles. The onset of the rapid TPC increase shifts from ⟨N⟩ ≈ 1 for 3.6-eV excitation to ⟨N⟩ ≈ 2 for 2.4-eV excitation, consistent with hot-electron generation by means of single-step and two-step SE-Auger upconversion, respectively. This behaviour is expected because ejection of a cold band-edge electron requires an energy of approximately 3.5 eV, which exceeds the energy released in a single SE-Auger event (about 2.1 eV) and therefore requires two sequential SE-mediated upconversion steps. b, Bias-dependent TPC traces (log–log representation) measured at a fixed transport distance of d = 25 μm and ⟨N⟩ ≈ 4. Carrier transit times (ttr), determined from power-law fits to the pre-transit and post-transit regions, are indicated by the red diamonds. c, Distance-dependent TPC traces measured at an applied bias of 100 V. Transit times are indicated by the red diamonds. d, Transit time plotted as a function of 10 d/F, in which F is the applied electric field, obtained from the data in panels b (red circles) and c (blue diamonds). The factor of 10 is introduced for convenient conversion of the fitted slope to mobility in cm2 V−1 s−1, as described in Fig. 5d. The linear fit (line) yields an average electron mobility of ⟨μe⟩ = 164 cm2 V−1 s−1, demonstrating that long-range, high-mobility transport is preserved under near-band-edge excitation. a.u., arbitrary units.

It has been revealed that comparison of early-time TA spectra of Mn-doped CdSe/CdS QDs measured in solution (1-mm optical path length) and in a 200-nm-thick solid-state film prepared using the same ligand-exchange procedure as used in the TPC experiments. The measurements were performed under identical excitation conditions: 3.6-eV, 150-fs pump pulses at an average excitation level of ⟨N⟩ = 0.3 and a pump–probe delay of Δt = 4 ps. In both samples, the band-edge bleach is centred at 2.35 eV, demonstrating that ligand exchange and film processing preserve the QD bandgap and, therefore, the quantum-confinement regime without evidence of QD sintering. The broader bleach observed in the film sample is attributed to the lower signal-to-noise ratio resulting from the much smaller optical density of the 200-nm film, which partially obscures the two closely spaced transitions involving the same 1Se electron level and the 1Sh,3/2 and 2Sh,3/2 hole states.

Sources indicate that a, Schematic of a TPC ToF experiment. A photoconductive gap is defined between two electrodes with edges at x = 0 and x = L. The centre of the focused laser beam is positioned at x = x0. The photoinjected electron packet drifts towards the charge-collecting electrode with velocity vd. b, Integrated photocurrent (circles) plotted as a function of the laser beam position (x0) within the photoconductive gap. The data were obtained for a heavily doped Mn:CdSe/CdS QD film at an excitation level of ⟨N⟩ = 5.12 excitons per dot per pulse (Supplementary Note 3). To exclude the initial spike arising from capacitive current, the integration window was restricted to 0.4–4.0 ns, corresponding to the dominant drift photocurrent component. The solid line is a fit using the model described by equation (S3.6) in Supplementary Note 3, from which the FWHM of the hot-electron packet is determined to be Γ1/2,hot = 41.5 μm. Consistent with the approximately cubic dependence of the hot-electron photocurrent on ⟨N⟩ (Fig. 2d, inset), this width is smaller than the original laser beam width (70–80 μm) by approximately a factor of \(\sqrt{3}\). a.u., arbitrary units.

THE BREAKDOWN: The real reasons why Enzo Maresca's Man City can't stop losing - from anonymous Enzo Fernandez abandoning Elliot Anderson, to the fatal flaws in Italian's set-up that are being brutally exposed

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 07:00 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 05:23 EST, 26 November 2026.
  • Enzo Maresca may look like Pep Guardiola, may have learned his craft under his Manchester City predecessor, but his quest to follow in his mentor’s footsteps has all gone a bit flat.
  • Seven successive Premier League wins to start his City reign, a record for a fresh manager in the competition, breaking one jointly-held by Guardiola, gave the impression that this might be a smooth passing of the torch after all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 07:00 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 05:23 EST, 26 November 2026.

Diet Pep is losing his fizz. Enzo Maresca may look like Pep Guardiola, may have learned his craft under his Manchester City predecessor, but his quest to follow in his mentor’s footsteps has all gone a bit flat.

Seven successive Premier League wins to start his City reign, a record for a fresh manager in the competition, breaking one jointly-held by Guardiola, gave the impression that this might be a smooth passing of the torch after all.

Three months in, and three defeats on the spin that left them six points behind Arsenal have made it clear that something is not clicking for Maresca.

According to recent reports, is the uncertainty around the potential punishment following that guilty verdict taking its toll? Is Maresca just suffering from his usual late autumn dips? He suffered similar tricky periods around late October and early November at Leicester and his first season at Chelsea too.

Or is there something at the heart of his side, of his system, that’s finally being exposed?

Enzo Maresca's Man City have slumped to three straight Premier League defeats after a promising start to the season.

Sources indicate that guardiola’s City was all about control. Keep the ball, dominate the pitch, play the game at your pace, on your terms.

Maresca’s City, regardless of how well they started the season, has been about anything but. It has been about triumph amid chaos, about moments of magic more than the overarching method.

Without that control, City’s defensive concerns have been laid bare. The 13 goals they have let in after 10 games is their most at this stage since 2008. They haven’t kept a clean sheet in their last eight matches in all competitions. That's a drought longer than at any point under Guardiola.

Their biggest problem over City's three successive Premier League defeats is just how susceptible they have been to counter attacks.

Only Newcastle have faced more shots this season following ‘fast breaks’ – data giants Opta's term for counter attacks – than City’s 17, and 11 of those have come in the last three games: six against Nottingham Forest, two of which led to goals, three against Brighton and another two against Aston Villa.

Maresca’s side are being more profligate in possession, too. Over the first seven games of the season, they lost the ball 120 times a game on average – one of the best figures in the division. Since then, it’s closer to 140.

City have been wasteful in possession and regularly overrun on the counter, with Elliot Anderson (centre) too often left isolated in midfield.

ANDERSON CAN'T DO IT ALL ON HIS OWN.

Many of these problems have their roots in Maresca's serious problems in midfield. Rodri, the best holding midfielder of his generation, was always going to be hard to replace but Maresca appears to be expecting Elliot Anderson to do it all on his own.

Sources indicate that anderson is at his best when he’s free to get up and down the pitch, box to box, using his physicality not just in winning the ball back but progressing it. No midfielder played more passes into the final third last season than Anderson at Forest. At one stage of the campaign, he had played more progressive passes than any other player across Europe’s top five leagues.

And yet Maresca is forcing Anderson to play as the sitter while his golden boy Enzo Fernandez, whom he pushed City to sign in the summer for £125million, is roaming free and high up the pitch.

Maresca likes his teams to build up in a 3-1-6 shape, which sees Fernandez push up as an extra attacking midfielder, and leaves Anderson manning the fort alone.

When City lose the ball, though, it leaves them wide open.

Industry observers note that this is the opening goal City conceded against Forest. Josko Gvardiol wants to play the ball inside but has only red shirts and empty green space ahead of him. Anderson is the only man free, but even he is too high and has a Forest player ready to cut off the pass. Eventually, Gvardiol gets robbed and Forest score.

According to recent reports, A lack of options for Josko Gvardiol (left) led to Forest's opener against City. Enzo Fernandez (circled) was caught high up the pitch, way ahead of the deeper Anderson (also circled).

Here’s another moment in the defeat by Brighton.

In a recent development, the Seagulls break forward on the flank and Anderson races over to close the ball down. Fernandez is, you guessed it, high up the pitch.

City have no midfield cover to stop the ball inside, Abdukodir Khusanov gets drawn in and leaves loads of space in behind for Yasin Ayari to exploit and cross to Maxim De Cuyper for a great chance.

The lack of protection offered by Anderson and especially the more advanced Fernandez was again on show against Brighton, who were able to exploit the acres of space left in midfield.

Fernandez is doing what Maresca wants, but it’s not working. Maresca needs more from him, especially when Anderson’s instincts are to press and harass and bully, which can leave gaps when he does not yet read the game as comprehensively as Rodri.

It has been revealed that anderson sits in the top five for ball recoveries among midfielders to have played 500 minutes this season. Fernandez is in the bottom five. That figure becomes even more alarming when you consider Anderson has created more chances from open play than Fernandez, too.

Ayyoub Bouaddi showed at the World Cup that he had the most similar profile to Rodri. It might be time for Maresca to put some faith in him.

Sources indicate that maresca has always wanted his goalkeeper to be an 11th outfielder. In his one season at Leicester, Mads Hermansen played more passes than any goalkeeper in Championship history. During his time at Chelsea, there was a shaky moment in a draw with Arsenal when loud groans greeted a misplaced pass from Robert Sanchez.

Recent findings suggest that ‘I am the guy who asks Robert to do that,’ said Maresca after that game. ‘The moment he stops doing that, he is not going to play.’.

Industry observers note that donnarumma, though, for all his (usually) excellent shot-stopping, is anything but a ball-playing goalkeeper. The ball rolled under his foot from a simple back pass against Coventry and so nearly crept over the line. He gifted France an early lead while on international duty with Italy when he passed the ball straight to Michael Olise.

Only two keepers made more errors leading to shots than Donnarumma across the course of last season, with many of those being with his feet, like when he gifted Kai Havertz an equaliser in City's victory over Arsenal in April.

Gianluigi Donnarumma has never been good with his feet - now his excellent shot-stopping has taken a dip too.

The Italian should have easily dealt with Nicolas Jackson's second goal in City's 2-1 loss at Aston Villa.

The decision to let James Trafford leave in the summer, especially with Guardiola’s impending departure and a manager like Maresca coming in, is looking ever more misguided.

In a recent development, trafford is not immune to mistakes either, of course. He erred badly when trying to play out from the back for City against Spurs last season and made an almost identical howler for Leeds at Bournemouth in October. But he is still far more confident at playing out from the back than Donnarumma.

The double blow for Maresca is that the trade-off with Donnarumma – where he makes up for his weakness with the ball at his feet by making saves that other keepers can’t make – is no longer paying off either.

Nicolas Jackson’s shot squirmed straight through him to hand Villa victory and condemn City to their first defeat of the season.

When you are coughing up chances as frequently as City are, Maresca needs his keeper to be on top form.

Do you know who is keeping the ball out of his net? James Trafford. He boasts the highest save percentage of any goalkeeper in the top flight, keeping out 81 per cent of the shots on target coming his way. Donnarumma is 15th, on less than 66 per cent.

According to Opta’s expected data, Trafford has also prevented more than four goals that he should have conceded from the quality of the shots he’s faced. Again, he’s the best in the Premier League. Donnarumma is middle of the pack.

According to recent reports, ‘At the moment, I’m not thinking about the goalkeeping situation,’ said Maresca recently. Without Trafford there and just 34-year-old Geronimo Rulli as back-up, he doesn’t really have a choice but to persist with Donnarumma and hope he improves.

When the goals stop flowing for Erling Haaland, City can't mask all their other problems.

So used are we now to seeing the Norwegian on the scoresheet, having notched nine in City’s opening eight matches, that when he goes just two games without a goal it feels as if he’s on a barren spell.

The matter, though, is less down to Haaland and more that City’s build-up in recent weeks is struggling to get him into the game.

City are finding it more difficult to get Haaland on the ball. His touches per game are falling steadily but, crucially, so are the quality of the chances his team-mates are creating for him.

Haaland had more than one Opta-defined 'big chance' in five of City’s opening seven games. He’s had just one come his way in each of their three defeats.

Industry observers note that his expected goals (xG) tally is dropping too. Across City’s winning streak, Haaland’s average xG per match was 0.81. Only once, against Liverpool, did it drop below 0.5.

Over the three defeats, it’s just 0.45 and has not once gone above 0.5.

Antoine Semenyo missing the last three games through injury has not helped, especially when teams now try to pack the middle of the pitch and force City wide.

Haaland will come good, he always does, but City need to start serving him again if Maresca wants to get through this tricky spell and stop the vultures from circling.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that janosch, the pen name of German author and illustrator Horst Eckert, won hearts around the world with his warm and simple sense of humor. He charmed children and adults alike with his iconic Tiger, Bear, Tiger-Duck and other animals.

Janosch created more than 150 books, which have been translated into over 30 languages.

His best-selling children's book, "Oh, wie schön ist Panama," translated into English as "The Trip to Panama," was so lucrative that Janosch was able to settle down on the Canary Island of Tenerife in 1980, where he lived together with his wife Ines. The writer and illustrator died peacefully at the age of 95, his publisher Bernhard Feil declared on Wednesday.

Sources indicate that janosch was born as Horst Eckert on March 11, 1931, in Hindenburg (now Zabrze, Poland) in what was then Upper Silesia. After World War II, his family had to flee to Germany.

Sources indicate that in 1953, Janosch started studying at the Academy of Art in Munich, thinking that it would be easy to become an artist. He was however dismissed after just a few terms for "lack of talent.".

Industry observers note that but luckily for his later readers, Janosch did not give up. He continued to work as a freelance artist, soon discovering his second great gift, namely writing.

His first children's book about a horse named Valek was published in 1960.

Although Janosch became famous primarily for his children's books, he also wrote books for adults that focused on his own childhood.

Even though he wrote cheerful books for children, Janosch hardly had any positive memories of his own childhood, as his father was an alcoholic. He was beaten not only by him but also by his mother and grandmother. Raised in a strictly Catholic environment, he was continuously threatened to be punished by God.

Later on, Janosch tried to overcome the burden of his childhood memories by turning to alcohol as well.

He always expressed a great deal of understanding for children, trying to encourage them to stand up for their rights. As a result of his childhood experiences, Janosch did not want to have children himself, and his attitude towards the Catholic Church always remained divided. "As I am a sinner and a heretic, God will let me live a long life so that I can return to the Church," he told his biographer Angela Bajorek.

It has been revealed that janosch's animal figures are endearing but not always well-behaved. They love all kinds of nonsense. But even if they lie to each other or put their own interests first, the true winner at the end of stories is always friendship and solidarity.

Recent findings suggest that janosch achieved his major breakthrough with "The Trip to Panama," a story about two friends, a little tiger and a bear, who set out to find their paradise in Panama. After touring around in circles, they finally end up where they started out; they realize that their journey was the destination. Janosch received the German Youth Book Prize in 1979 for the work.

In a recent development, janosch's protagonists have become familiar to generations of children all over the world. They come up over and over again in the various stories carefully illustrated with water colors.

Sources indicate that there is the honest lion Hans from the toy chest who fails to catch a nutcracker with his lies. There is Schnuddel and a ridiculous bragger Günter the Box-Frog. And then there is a tiger that collects mushrooms while looking out for his devoted friend, a bear, who always stands up for him even when the tiger temporarily leaves him because of a little pig in one of the stories.

The "Tigerente," literally "Tiger-Duck," a wooden duck on wheels with yellow-brown stripes, appears on numerous pictures by the illustrator. At times, the animal has been tossed into a corner, at times it is hanging from the ceiling, or the Box-Frog pulls it across the drawing.

His iconic figures, especially the Tiger-Duck, have served as motifs on various items, from cups to stamps to jewelry, and even on airplanes. Film adaptations and TV series based on his stories were produced in German and English.

Guests who visited Janosch in Tenerife were impressed by his very modest lifestyle. He always said that hanging around in his hammock doing nothing was what he enjoyed most. And yet Janosch remained very active until the end of his life.

From 2013 to 2019, he wrote a column for the German weekly Die Zeit, taking on the role of Mr. Wondrak, who commented on world affairs. Shortly before his 90th birthday in 2021, the complete collection of his Mr. Wondrak columns were published as a book in German.

Like the protagonists in his stories, Janosch always tried to content himself with few things. As he wrote in one of his books: "He who needs almost nothing, has everything.".

This article was originally written in German.

  • According to recent reports, sage replaced Oliver Glasner as manager in June but since then Palace have won just two league matches with him in at the helm.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pierre Sage has admitted that he fears for his future at Crystal Palace, adding that he felt “shame” after his side slumped to their joint-heaviest defeat by rivals Brighton and Hove Albion.

According to recent reports, sage replaced Oliver Glasner as manager in June but since then Palace have won just two league matches with him in at the helm. The south London club have taken seven points from seven Premier League games and have already conceded 17 goals, the most of any team in the league.

“I don’t know,” Sage remarked when asked if he will get enough time to rectify Palace’s slump. He admitted that his shame was about how Palace were overwhelmed, leaking three goals within the first nine minutes of the game before eventually losing 5-0.

In a recent development, “We are not at the level we expected, and I’m really sorry for that,” the 47-year-old said. “I just want to apologise to the fans because it’s not normal to show this face.”.

The Frenchman said that he took full responsibility for the 5-0 defeat, and understood why hundreds of Palace fans left well before the final whistle.

“I cannot blame anybody because we didn’t do the job in a good way,” he remarked. “I’m responsible for this team, and when the team play as today, it’s not normal. It’s my fault. I understand them.

“Another feeling is about shame because that’s my feeling after the game and from the beginning. It’s not normal to not respect the necessary of this kind of game.”.

Sage admitted that he will be assessing how Palace need to rethink their approach in the coming fixtures, beginning with Thursday’s trip to Besiktas in the Europa League.

“The first work to do is on me,” he said. “I’m responsible for what’s happened on the pitch, and I have a lot of work to do because I have to change this kind of thing.

“It’s maybe in the preparation, in the way we give them the motivation to start the game just before in the locker room in the warm-up. We have to analyse that because it’s not normal. And today it was really at the highest level we cannot expect, and that’s the moment to change the thing.”.

According to recent reports, for all the scrutiny on his back three, Sage urged his entire side to take greater defensive responsibility, highlighting how the team were too passive in pressing Brighton. Palace have struggled to regain the solidity that long characterised the side since the departures of Marc Guéhi in January and Maxence Lacroix this summer.

“The way of defending is not only on the back three; it is for every player, and there are some things to do collectively, too,” Sage mentioned. “When we defend low we struggle a lot.”.

Sage joined Palace after a fine campaign with Lens. He led the club to second place in Ligue 1, just six points off Paris St-Germain, and victory in the Coupe de France. Yet, despite Sage’s reputation when he moved to Selhurst Park, his suitability for the Palace job is increasingly being questioned.

Industry observers note that three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Sage could suffer the same fate, with doubts growing that he will still be in charge for Thursday’s trip to Besiktas.

It has been revealed that “It’s not my decision,” Sage said. “I don’t want to accept the level of the moment if we are able to do better. And today the work is really vital to do, and I will do it. It’s my job, and I’d like to change this.”.

In a recent development, with only Manchester City and Arsenal above them, Brighton and Hove Albion are entitled to dream of making history. Yet, whatever happens between now and May, one accolade is already surely their own: the goal of the season award.

Diego Gómez’s 56-yard strike will instantly become the stuff of Brighton lore. The Paraguayan’s audacity will be even more cherished for coming against Crystal Palace, who were pummelled 5-0 in the M23 derby.

All Premier League defeats are equal but some are more equal than others. Three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Pierre Sage is at grave risk of suffering the same fate. Naturally, Brighton fans revelled in reminding him of this threat as the final whistle approached.Palace were so ragged that their performance felt like a defeat that marks the end of a managerial reign. Even stand-in captain Adam Wharton was guilty of dawdling and losing the ball in possession. Hundreds of away supporters left well before the full-time whistle and those who remained booed all players bar Jefferson Lerma.

With less venom in attack, especially with Ismaïla Sarr being an unused substitute, Palace’s sole chance lay in counter-attacking. This strategy disintegrated in the fourth minute, when Jaydee Canvot headed Pascal Gross’s free-kick into his own net.

Jaydee Canvot glances the ball into his own net and Brighton lead! 🔵 https://t.co/subm9ggwId.

But the hint of self-immolation in Palace’s display should not obscure the swagger of Brighton’s performance. Despite losing Danny Welbeck, last year’s top scorer, Brighton have scored 23 goals already this Premier League campaign, the most in the league. This tally includes one of the most extraordinary goals in Premier League history.

Most simply, Gómez’s goal, which put Brighton 2-0 up in the seventh minute, was a triumph of the imagination. Receiving a short pass from Olivier Boscagli just inside his own half, Gómez could have sought to pick out a team-mate. Instead, his scanning of the pitch before receiving the ball had revealed that goalkeeper Walter Benítez was off his line and Brighton’s attacking players were being tightly guarded by defenders. And so, just as he entered the centre circle in the opposition half, Gómez attempted the absurd.

In a recent development, "Would you look at that!" DIEGO GOMEZ SCORES FROM THE HALFWAY LINE! 🤯 https://t.co/qmagVbGEb4.

In a recent development, “I’m not training with Diego Gómez shooting from 50 metres in training,” head coach Fabian Hürzeler stated while breaking into a smile. “It’s just about making the players quick in their minds.

“In these moments it’s about being very precise with his long kick. The perception to recognise the keeper and being quick to go to the action was impressive.”.

According to recent reports, the presence of mind to attempt something outlandish was one thing; the execution was quite another. With Benítez vulnerable, Gómez took just one touch with his right foot before taking his shot, not giving the keeper enough time to scramble back to cover his line. As he looked up to confirm the opportunity, the 23-year-old struck the ball over Benítez with such venom that it did not even bounce until it reached the goal.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the M23 derby – or El Gatwicko, as the kids call it these days – as high-flying Brighton and Hove Albion host Crystal Palace at the Amex Stadium. Being frank, this is neither the fiercest nor the most storied Premier League rivalry, but few would have imagined when these sides faced off in the Third Division in the mid-1970s that this would ever become a top-flight match-up sandwiched between European games.

Brighton have been outstanding this season and took their league form into the Conference League, thrashing Lithuanian champions Kauno Zalgiris on Thursday night. Fabian Hürzeler was delighted by his fringe players’ performances on Thursday night and may have some selection questions to answer with Jack Hinshelwood and Georginio Rutter finding the net. Brighton are third in the Premier League and were the division’s heaviest scorers after the last round of matches.

Yet the Palace nut has been a tough one to crack for Hürzeler, having not yet registered a win in four attempts. When asked what he enjoyed most about the rivalry, the German mentioned: “Nothing yet, because I didn’t win any games so far. Hopefully on Sunday this changes… I like these games because they’re derbies, more emotions, it’s a rivalry, it’s [us] against Crystal Palace.”.

Industry observers note that in his pre-match interview Hürzeler admitted to being an admirer of Pierre Sage, and while the Frenchman’s side have failed to match Brighton’s fast start, they rallied impressively to defeat rivals Nottingham Forest last weekend and fought back valiantly away at Lyon, albeit in a losing effort, in midweek. The return of Ismaïla Sarr from injury is a significant boost.

Sources indicate that elsewhere Bournemouth host Sunderland hoping to secure their first Premier League victory of the season. Marco Rose’s side and Tottenham are the only teams still without a win, but Bournemouth have been perfect in the Europa League and will look to transfer some of that momentum into the league. Sunderland scored late to win away at Portuguese side Torreense.

You can also follow the latest updates from Manchester United’s crucial trip to Elland Road in our sister blog here.
