📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Calum Burrowes | 26 Nov 2026 10:55, Last updated: 26 Nov 2026 20:05.

Two former Arsenal teammates come head to head on Saturday in League One as in-form Luton Town welcome high-flying Oxford United to Kenilworth Road.

Jack Wilshere's side will be looking to extend their unbeaten run to nine matches in all competitions after coming from behind to win 2-1 last weekend, while Aaron Ramsey and his U's will be aiming to move into the automatic promotion places by securing a fourth win in five third-tier outings.

More than six months after Luton Town narrowly missed out on a place in the League One playoffs last season, finishing just one point behind sixth-placed Leyton Orient, the Hatters have made a positive start to the 2026-27 campaign as they look to go one step better this time around.

Wilshere's side began the new season inconsistently and were sitting 16th after seven third-tier matches at the end of September, but have since enjoyed an impressive upturn in form, losing just once in the league across October and November, a 2-1 defeat to MK Dons at Stadium MK.

That run has seen Luton win six of their last eight league matches, while also progressing to the second round of the FA Cup and the knockout stages of the EFL Trophy, putting them firmly back in the playoff picture.

In fact, the Hatters could move into second place heading into the final month of the calendar year if they secure a ninth league victory of the season and other results go their way this weekend, with their recent form having lifted them more than 10 places into fifth and guaranteed them a place in the top six until at least their 17th league match next week, when they face struggling Blackpool.

A key factor behind their turnaround has been an improvement in front of goal, with Luton scoring 17 times in League One since the start of October, an average of more than two per game that has taken their overall tally to 29, a record bettered by just one side in the division.

As for the visitors, Oxford United make the 66-mile journey to Bedfordshire in similarly strong form and will be looking to move into December in the top two by recording a third consecutive victory.

The U's, led by former Wales midfielder Ramsey, have enjoyed a more consistent campaign than their upcoming opponents, having already moved into the top six by their seventh match of the 2026-27 season, when Luton were sitting 16th, and have continued to build on that strong start in recent weeks to climb to third.

Oxford head into their 15th league outing of the season with 29 points following eight wins, five draws and just one defeat, and they could move level on points with leaders Stockport County this weekend while still having two games in hand on Jimmy McNulty's side.

Although Oxford's FA Cup campaign came to an end at the first hurdle with a 1-0 home defeat to Stevenage, their form in the third tier has been exceptional, with no side in the top four divisions of English football losing fewer league matches than the U's.

Only Ramsey and Wilshere's former club Arsenal and League Two side Barnet have matched their tally of just one defeat.

While Luton have built their campaign around a clinical attacking unit, Oxford's promotion push has been underpinned by a strong defensive record, with only three sides in League One having conceded fewer than their 14 goals.

However, shipping three at home to Wycombe Wanderers last weekend, despite coming from three goals behind to secure a remarkable 4-3 victory, represented a rare blemish on an otherwise impressive defensive campaign.

The pair meet for the first time in just under two years on Saturday and will lock horns in a third-tier fixture for the first time since 2019, with Luton having enjoyed a spell in the Premier League since their previous meeting at this level.

Luton Town form (all competitions):.

Oxford United form (all competitions):.

Luton Town will be forced into at least one change following their weekend victory over Burton Albion after Jordan Clark was forced off with an injury in the 33rd minute, with the midfielder expected to miss out and potentially be replaced by Daniel Gore.

Clark is set to join fellow injury absentees Hakeem Odoffin, Gideon Kodua and Shayden Morris in the treatment room, with the latter yet to feature at all this season.

Former Bristol City forward Nahki Wells marked his 15th league appearance of the campaign with his eighth and ninth goals of the season, scoring a brace against the Brewers last Saturday, and the Bermudian is expected to lead the line once again.

Having been in EFL Trophy action during the week, beating Tottenham Hotspur Under-21s 2-1, Ramsey is expected to make wholesale changes for Oxford's return to League One action.

Jamie Cumming started in goal for the midweek cup tie and could retain his place ahead of Simon Eastwood, who conceded three times last weekend, while changes are also expected throughout the defence, midfield and attack.

Gatlin O'Donkor came off the bench to score a dramatic winner five minutes into stoppage time against Wycombe and could therefore be rewarded with a starting place on Saturday, potentially at the expense of Tyler Goodrham.

Shea; Jones, Mengi, Andersen, Johnston; Walsh; Richards, Donley, Gore, Palmer; Wells.

Oxford United possible starting lineup:.

Cumming; Kioso, Long, Brown, Currie; Brannagan, Andrews; Missanga, O'Donkor, Emakhu; Harris.

While Oxford United arrive at Kenilworth Road in high spirits, they face a side who have collected more points than any other team in the division across their last six league games, meaning the U's will know they face a difficult task to win at a ground where they have not tasted victory since 2017.

With that remarked, Oxford did manage to come away from their last visit to Luton with a point, albeit more than two years ago, and we expect them to repeat that feat, with the two in form sides playing out a 2-2 draw.

Nice vs. Troyes - prediction, team news, lineups

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Seye Omidiora | 26 Nov 2026 10:58.
  • Nice return to Ligue 1 action a week after Paris Saint-Germain ended their three-match winning streak, with promoted Troyes visiting Allianz Riviera on matchday 12.
  • The Europe-chasing hosts remain one of the division's form teams and will back themselves to overcome a promoted side they have beaten in their last three meetings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Seye Omidiora | 26 Nov 2026 10:58.

Nice return to Ligue 1 action a week after Paris Saint-Germain ended their three-match winning streak, with promoted Troyes visiting Allianz Riviera on matchday 12.

The Europe-chasing hosts remain one of the division's form teams and will back themselves to overcome a promoted side they have beaten in their last three meetings.

Olivier Pantaloni and his players faced a formidable challenge against PSG last weekend, with the defending Ligue 1 champions arriving on a seven-match winning streak.

While PSG extended their sequence of top-flight victories to eight, Nice's three-match winning run ended against the Parisians, hardly a disgrace given their opponents' quality and form.

Les Aiglons remain one of Ligue 1's form teams, with their 12 points from the last available 18 surpassed by only three clubs: PSG (18), Marseille (15) and Brest (13).

Back at home just days after PSG ended their eight-month unbeaten run on their own turf, Pantaloni's men will target maximum points to reclaim a European place, with sixth-placed Brest and fifth-placed Marseille sitting one and two points above Nice respectively.

That ambition appears reasonable given the Eaglets' three consecutive victories in this fixture and four wins in the last five meetings, with the visitors needing a strong performance to beat Nice at Allianz Riviera for the first time since 2017.

Stephane Dumont's men will fancy their chances of a positive result as they enter matchday 12 having collected six points from the last available nine.

Their only defeat during that period was an understandable 1-0 reverse at PSG, a performance that offered ESTAC encouragement in their bid to avoid an immediate return to Ligue 2.

Troyes' recent improvement follows a six-match winless run that included five consecutive defeats, with last season's Ligue 2 champions failing to score in four of those losses.

Collecting six points from their recent fixtures has lifted them out of the relegation zone and into 14th, although Dumont's men sit just one point above Strasbourg in the relegation playoff spot and three clear of second-bottom Angers.

While a disastrous weekend could leave the top-flight returnees in the bottom three, that would require victories for Auxerre, Strasbourg and Angers, with the latter also needing a six-goal swing.

Mohamed Abdelmonem (hamstring) and Elye Wahi are doubtful, although the six-goal forward is expected to feature for the hosts this weekend.

Laurent Abergel and Antoine Mendy remain unavailable due to long-term knee injuries, while Moise Bombito is also sidelined with a leg problem.

Beyond Wahi, Jonathan Clauss (three goals, three assists), Mohamed Amoura (three goals, two assists) and Sofiane Diop (two goals, three assists) all possess match-winning quality for the Eaglets.

Troyes' leading attacking threats are last weekend's two-goal hero Antoine Mille and Renaud Ripart, who remain the visitors' only players to have scored more than once in 2026-27.

Merwan Ifnaoui faces a pre-match assessment to determine his availability this weekend, while Paolo Gozzi (hamstring) and Yacouba Kone (knee) are sidelined.

Diouf; Seidu, Ndayishimiye, Mandza; Clauss, Witsel, Boudaoui, Nkounkou; Diop, Amoura; Wahi.

Troyes possible starting lineup:.

Konate; Maronnier, Monfray, Diaz, Boura; Ifnaoui, Diop, Mille, Karim, Diawara; Ripart.

Troyes' six-point return from their last three matches and narrow defeat at PSG suggest that Nice should expect a more demanding assignment than the visitors' promoted status might imply.

However, the Eaglets have several reliable attacking contributors and have our backing to respond to last weekend's setback with a fourth consecutive victory in this fixture.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Carter White | 26 Nov 2026 11:09.

Premier League clubs are reportedly interested in signing Fenerbahce defender Archie Brown during the January transfer window.

The 24-year-old has followed in the footsteps of Jude Bellingham and Jobe Bellingham in recent years, leaving the English domestic scene to forge a successful football career on the continent.

Brown has been a regular appearance-maker for the Turkish giants this season and played the full 90 minutes on Wednesday night, when the Turkish Super Lig club beat Shakhtar Donetsk in the Champions League.

With his performances catching the eye in Europe this term, Fenerbahce man Brown is supposedly admired by a number of high-profile clubs, including Nottingham Forest of the Premier League.

The highlight of the youngster's season so far undoubtedly arrived on November 4 when he found the net and provided an assist during the Yellow Canaries' 3-2 Champions League success over Liverpool.

According to German transfer specialist Florian Plettenberg, Fenerbahce defender Brown is attracting interest from across the continent following an impressive opening to the 2026-27 season.

The report claims that a number of Premier League clubs are keen on bringing the 24-year-old back to English shores, with the winter transfer window opening at the turn of the calendar year on January 1.

Providing encouragement for those sides eyeing up a swoop for Brown, the left-back supposedly has a release clause totalling £19.2m in his current contract with the Super Lig powerhouses.

It is understood that the stipulation can be triggered either during the upcoming January or summer transfer windows, meaning that potential suitors have options in their hunt for the player.

Since a 2-1 home defeat by Goztepe on October 31, Brown and Fenerbahce have strung together a four-game unbeaten run (W3 D1), a streak which includes that historic home success over Liverpool.

Brown spent a large chunk of his academy time within the ranks of East Midlands club Derby County, making 27 appearances for their Under-21s side before commencing his professional career abroad.

The 23-year-old started at Swiss outfit Lausanne in the Swiss Super League following a switch in June 2021, playing 43 matches and scoring five goals across a two-year stint at Stade de la Tuiliere.

The former Rams youngsters truly made a name for himself at Belgium side Gent before securing a high-profile transfer to Turkish and European giants Fenerbahce during the summer of 2025.

Francesco Camarda has spoken about his Champions League goal that never was today, and how it was an AC Milan dream come true.

Recent findings suggest that camarda first became known to Milan as a youngster, but he confirmed himself further when he became Serie A’s youngest-ever appearance maker. He almost then went to a European level, with a goal in the Champions League. However, it wasn’t to be.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Industry observers note that on his debut in the competition, the starlet bagged a goal which would’ve made him the Rossoneri’s youngest-ever scorer in Europe’s main stage. Yet it was ruled out for offside and a few years on, the now 18-year-old is still waiting for a first competitive goal for the Diavolo.

Speaking to Vice, the striker opened up about his dream of playing in the Champions League at San Siro, his emotions after his goal (and it later being disallowed) and how his teammates rallied around him, as MilanVibes relayed.

“As a child, I used to say to my dad: imagine if one day I could walk into San Siro and hear the Champions League anthem, accompanied by the roar of the entire stadium. When it actually happened, I thought back to that little boy and realised I had realised a dream.

In a recent development, “When I stepped onto the pitch, I had an incredible adrenaline rush. Then the goal came, and I felt the whole stadium explode. I also felt the affection of my teammates, who immediately raised me into the air.

“However, when I looked at the scoreboard and saw that the VAR check was in progress, I was already convinced the goal would be disallowed.

It has been revealed that “When I returned home that evening, with my parents and cousin, I burst into tears. I was overjoyed by the goal, but at the same time deeply disappointed by what had happened. It wasn’t easy at first, but I also worked on my mental health and managed to put that moment behind me.

“Today, I’m proud of the journey I’ve taken and of having overcome those difficulties.”.

“I remember what Gabbia told me: he was sorry for what happened, but he explained that the experience should give me even more motivation. It should push me to improve, to train harder, and to work so I can relive even more wonderful emotions.”.

Industry observers note that “In football, there are positive and negative opinions; it has always been this way and will continue to be this way. A player’s true strength lies in not being influenced by what is said, because, regardless of whether you do well or badly, someone will always find a reason to judge you.”.

Breaking: Harry Potter films turns 25 ahead of latest TV series' release

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that on November 4, 2001, London's Leicester Square became a world of witches and wizards.
  • "Thousands of excited fans, some dressed up in wizard hats and cloaks, gathered to catch a glimpse of arriving celebrities," the BBC reported at the time.
  • Daniel Radcliffe, who played Harry Potter, was just 12 years old and clearly impressed by the spectacle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that on November 4, 2001, London's Leicester Square became a world of witches and wizards. The occasion was the world premiere of "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" (released in the US and India as "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone").

"Thousands of excited fans, some dressed up in wizard hats and cloaks, gathered to catch a glimpse of arriving celebrities," the BBC reported at the time.

Daniel Radcliffe, who played Harry Potter, was just 12 years old and clearly impressed by the spectacle. The BBC quoted him as saying, "It is so cool. I have never heard my name shouted so much in an hour.".

The crowds showed just how far Harry Potter fever had spread in only four years.

The first Harry Potter book was published by Britain's Bloomsbury in June 1997, with an initial print run of just 500 hardcover copies.

About 5,000 paperback copies were also released around the same time.

Today, first editions are prized collectors' items, with hardcover copies commanding high prices at auction. In mid-October, one sold for $400,000 through US auction house Heritage Auctions.

At first, the book's popularity grew largely by word of mouth among schoolchildren. Media attention followed when it won the prestigious Nestle Smarties Book Prize later that year.

With an estimated 120 million-plus copies sold worldwide, it is the best-selling book in the series and ranks among the best-selling novels of all time.

For years, J.K. Rowling's public image was defined by her extraordinary rise from a single mother on welfare to a billionaire.

Industry observers note that but in recent years, debate over her views on gender and transgender identity has increasingly overshadowed that success. It's an issue Rowling herself frequently weighs in on.

In a recent development, in an essay published on her website on October 21, 2026, Rowling reiterated her opposition to what she calls the "current, dominant strain of trans activism." She argues that this movement "holds that a man who declares himself a woman is, literally, a woman, and is therefore entitled to be treated as a woman in all contexts." Rowling argues that allowing trans women into single-sex spaces poses a risk. She describes biological sex as an indisputable biological fact.

Such statements have led critics to accuse Rowling of transphobia, while others regard her stance as a defense of women's rights and safety.

The controversy has also divided her fans. Some stand by Rowling, while others try to draw a distinction between the books and their author.

Sources indicate that others have left Harry Potter behind altogether. One former fan is German YouTuber Coldmirror, known for her Harry Potter parodies. The media artist from the Bremen area, whose real name is Kathrin Fricke, told the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper: "I don't have any love left for Harry. I'm still somewhat interested, but I can no longer watch it in good conscience." She cited Rowling's campaigning against transgender people as the reason.

It has been revealed that the "Harry Potter" film cast is divided as well. The three main stars — Daniel Radcliffe, Emma Watson and Rupert Grint — have publicly spoken out in support of transgender people. Meanwhile, Ralph Fiennes, who played Lord Voldemort, and Helena Bonham Carter, who portrayed Bellatrix Lestrange, have defended Rowling's right to express her views.

Industry observers note that despite the controversy surrounding Rowling, Warner Bros., which holds the Harry Potter film rights, is bringing the books back to the screen — this time as a series for HBO. The premiere is scheduled for December 25.

The eight-episode first season is an an adaption of the first book. Even though the episode lengths haven't been unveiled, the scope of a TV series gives each book much more room than the original films did. That means more time to explore subplots, character development and everyday life at Hogwarts. While many fans are looking forward to a more detailed adaptation, others remain skeptical. They find it hard to imagine the familiar characters being played by anyone else.

The new trio consists of Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter, Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger and Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley.

J.K. Rowling is an executive producer on the show. HBO says, however, that her views on gender identity won't be reflected in the storyline. Several people involved in the latest production have publicly distanced themselves from her views. Paapa Essiedu, who has been cast as Severus Snape, signed an open letter supporting transgender people. Rowling subsequently noted she had neither the power nor the desire to have him removed from the show because of it. John Lithgow, who plays Dumbledore, and Nick Frost, who portrays Hagrid, have also spoken out against Rowling's views.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, the Harry Potter merchandising machine is still going strong. On November 4, Britain's largest Harry Potter store to date is set to open in London. According to Warner Bros., the two-story shop covers more than 1,950 square meters.

This article was originally written in German.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Darren Plant | 26 Nov 2026 11:30.
  • FC Cincinnati play host to Nashville SC on Saturday night looking to book their place in the conference semi-finals of the MLS Cup playoffs.
  • The home side hold a 1-0 advantage in the best-of-three tie having earned a surprise victory on away soil in the opening fixture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Darren Plant | 26 Nov 2026 11:30.

FC Cincinnati play host to Nashville SC on Saturday night looking to book their place in the conference semi-finals of the MLS Cup playoffs.

The home side hold a 1-0 advantage in the best-of-three tie having earned a surprise victory on away soil in the opening fixture.

Having booked their place in the MLS Cup playoffs as far back as September 19, the assumption was that Nashville SC would have too much quality for FC Cincinnati, who finished the regular Eastern Conference campaign with 31 fewer points.

Nashville had also defeated Cincinnati in the final game of the regular season by a 2-0 scoreline on away territory.

Nevertheless, an early own goal from Nashville midfielder Patrick Yazbek gave Cincinnati a 1-0 victory at Geodis Park on November 22.

That marked Nashville's first defeat since September 10, ending a 10-match unbeaten streak that featured seven wins and three draws.

B. J. Callaghan will have concerns that their efforts throughout 2026 are close to going to waste, with Nashville having failed to score in two of their last four matches.

However, Nashville make the trip to the TQL Stadium on a five-game unbeaten run on their travels, while just 11 goals were conceded in 17 regular season away contests.

As far as Cincinnati are concerned, they netted 39 goals from the same amount of home matches, the third best attacking return in home fixtures in the Eastern Conference.

Despite finishing down in ninth place, 10 points came from their closing five fixtures, and Pat Noonan's team have now emerged victorious from five of their last seven games, albeit only losing to Nashville in this exact fixture on November 7.

Prior to the first leg, Cincinnati had the benefit of shaking off a lack of match sharpness through registering a 3-1 win at Orlando City SC in the Eastern Conference wildcard tie.

FC Cincinnati Major League Soccer form:.

Nashville SC Major League Soccer form:.

Former Manchester United left-back Tyrell Malacia is an option to replace Bryan Ramirez at left wing-back for FC Cincinnati.

Tom Barlow, with 10 goals and five assists during the regular season, may also be introduced into the final third, but Noonan is not expected to overly-tinker with a winning team.

Meanwhile, Jack Maher could be brought into the Nashville SC backline after Maxwell Woledzi suffered an injury during the second half of the last game.

Yazbek and Bryan Acosta are battling for one place in central midfield, while Warren Madrigal may be recalled on the flank.

Sam Surridge, who has netted 21 league goals this season, has scored five times in his last seven appearances.

FC Cincinnati possible starting lineup:.

Celentano; Doudera, Malatini, Robinson, Smith, Malacia; Martinez, Gidi; Nwobodo; Evander, Denkey.

Nashville SC possible starting lineup:.

Schwake; Najar, Maher, Palacios, Baker-Whiting; Yazbek, Corcoran; Espinoza, Mukhtar, Saad; Surridge.

Although FC Cincinnati will be confident of making home territory count, we can only anticipate an improved performance from the Eastern Conference regular season winners. With that in mind, Nashville could edge this fixture by the odd goal in three to take the tie to a decider.

Published: 08:00 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 10:10 EST, 26 November 2026.

Wesley Fofana has apologised to Chelsea for his unauthorised interview and the club now consider the matter ‘closed’, with Xabi Alonso saying it is time to take things 'seriously'.

Fofana spoke with a French YouTuber called Zack Nani and within the two-hour conversation, the centre back laughed off his penalty miss which condemned the club to their Carabao Cup exit. Chelsea were beaten in a shootout by Liverpool last month after he skied his decisive spot-kick.

Fofana also revealed how his representatives advised him to honour his lucrative contract, worth £200,000 per week, when he was tempted to quit football amid his injury hell. Both revelations sparked a backlash from supporters online.

Alonso confirmed that Chelsea had spoken privately with Fofana, and the manager noted: ‘We have addressed that with him and for sure, it was unfortunate.

According to recent reports, ‘He apologised. He knows it was not right, the moment, and it was not right, the content. We are here to take things seriously and he said that it's not going to be repeated. We know that it's something that we don't want, these kind of things. They are not going to be repeated for sure.’.

When asked if that is case closed or if he will now be unavailable, Alonso noted: ‘Closed.’.

Wesley Fofana has apologised after angering Chelsea fans with his interview on French YouTube channel.

Fofana smashed his penalty over the bar against Liverpool in October but saw the funny side.

The YouTuber who conducted the ill-timed interview hit back at the coverage in England of Fofana’s quotes. Specifically, he was unhappy with how the focus was on Fofana joking about his penalty miss at Liverpool and what he said about considering retiring from football. That was despite the YouTuber’s own social media channel posting those precise clips which led to widespread criticism.

Regardless, Fofana has now seen fit to apologise to Chelsea, but it remains to be seen whether Alonso will stick with the Frenchman and Levi Colwill for Friday’s trip to Nottingham Forest.

In a recent development, both Fofana and Colwill were bullied by Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey and Leeds United’s Dominic Calvert-Lewin, and Liam Delap is the next challenge. Alonso spoke of the ‘standards’ needed from his central defenders to deal with such strikers.

Sources indicate that ‘That's the standards of the Premier League and for sure, it's an vital thing that we have spoken about,’ Alonso said. ‘That we need to show much better, to do much better, because if you don’t, then you are not able to control important situations in the game.’.

Delap will have a point to prove versus Chelsea, who sold him to Forest after a single season for £50million.

Vincenzo Montella’s time with AC Milan was ‘a dream’ for him, but he failed to achieve much during his time at the helm.

Sources indicate that looking back on Montella’s time leading Milan is tricky. On paper, the Italian had a strong tenure at the club, achieving a 50% win rate and only losing 18 of his 64 games in charge at San Siro, not a terrible record by any means.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

He even ended a five-year trophy drought with a win against Juventus in the Supercoppa Italiana and returned the Rossoneri to Europe, with a sixth-place finish in the 2016/17 season. In itself, that was a first since 2014.

It has been revealed that this is where context matters, though. The start of the 2017/18 season was tough, as the Diavolo won six of their first 14 games and he was sacked before December. Despite that, he still views the club in an excellent light.

Speaking to La Gazzetta dello Sport’s ‘La Tripletta’ podcast, Montella went over his time with the club and how he fulfilled a dream by taking the job, as MilanPress relays.

“It was a fantastic experience there [at Milan] too, it was my dream. Then, as a professional, it’s a little different, but when I was thirteen I was a fan of that AC Milan team. My older brother took me to see Maradona’s Napoli team twice to make me a Napoli fan, and Maradona scored three goals.

“Despite this, my idol was Van Basten because I was a striker: I studied him and dreamed of becoming like him, and so I was a Milan fan. I knew everything about Milan, so for me it was an incredible feeling to join Milan.”.

“He liked to talk about football; he liked to give advice even when it was a bit out of context at the time, because he always had the mentality of having Van Basten as a centre forward with Papin, a two-time Ballon d’Or winner, on the bench. He wanted me to play with two strikers, and I tried to plug the gap for months.

In a recent development, “I told him it was difficult; I knew all the lineups of those years. I was a Milan fan: the starter was Van Basten and the reserve was Papin, both Ballon d’Or winners. So, ‘If you buy me some players like that, rest assured that I’ll play them both.'”.

Recent findings suggest that “It was a year when we returned to Europe. I think it had been two or three years since Milan had been there, and it was something new at the time. We won a trophy, a small one. Just the other night I saw Galliani at a dinner; he reminded me of it and remembers it perfectly.

“I have to say that I found him to be the perfect manager at the time, because he was always on my side when it came to pressure; he gave me complete autonomy in my decisions and he helped me with everything, from the number of collaborators to latest things; whatever I asked for, he was always on the coach’s side.

“And so for me he was truly an incredible manager, who in that phase, in that change, was fundamental even in achieving these small results, especially after Berlusconi’s great AC Milan.

In a recent development, “We deserved to win even in regulation time: we had some easy chances to win it, then it came to penalties. Gigio saved the penalty from Dybala, who kicked it really hard, but he filled the net with it.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I was a little worried from the beginning because there was this obsession with publicising everything, almost like a publicity stunt, so I was a little worried. In theory, there was sharing, at least that’s what it looked like, but I couldn’t back out when in reality that wasn’t always the case.

“And so sometimes there were players I hadn’t even consulted about, who would arrive and then say, ‘It was shared,’ and when you’re there, you can’t say otherwise. Certainly, when you build a team and have the budget, the first thing you do is: we had a goalkeeper, I’ll get a centre forward, we were missing a centre forward.

In a recent development, “In the final selection, the centre forward was the only one left, with a budget of 15-20 million. And then Kalinic… yes, I chose him because that was the final budget. So our, let’s say, second-choice striker was paid thirty-eight million, if I remember correctly, who was André Silva, and the first striker was paid half that.

“And so, in my opinion, a misunderstanding of this kind was created, with so many changes, even though at that stage we weren’t even playing badly for having fifteen new players.

Industry observers note that “We still had Calhanoglu, who wasn’t feeling well, coming off months of suspension. The team was still being built: we weren’t in line with the Scudetto objectives that had been declared, but certainly, given our development, we were absolutely on target.

“Who would I have signed up front? At the time, we were probably negotiating for Aubameyang, if I remember correctly. Ronaldo? No, I didn’t believe it, not at all.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Adepoju Marvellous | 26 Nov 2026 11:46, Last updated: 26 Nov 2026 11:48.

Palmeiras and Estudiantes meet on Saturday afternoon in the 2026 Copa Libertadores final.

The clash at the iconic Estadio Centenario revives memories of the 1968 final, when Estudiantes claimed the first of their four titles and became the first Argentine side to beat a Brazilian team in the final.

Palmeiras, meanwhile, are chasing a fourth continental title after reaching three of the last six finals.

According to recent reports, after 58 years, Palmeiras have the chance to renew their rivalry with Estudiantes in a final worthy of the occasion. The 1968 final was decided over three matches: the Argentines won the first leg in La Plata before losing at the old Pacaembu.

In the decider at the same Estadio Centenario, Estudiantes won 2-0, with goals from Ribaudo and Juan Ramon Veron. One of the goals in Estudiantes’ first Libertadores triumph was scored by the father of the club’s current president, Juan Sebastian Veron.

Recent findings suggest that palmeiras have not been as dominant in 2026 as in previous years. They drew two of their six group-stage matches, but have taken the lead in eight of their last 10 continental fixtures during the knockout rounds.

In the round of 16, the Alviverde gained revenge on Cerro Porteno, completing a quartet of meetings between the sides this campaign.

Abel Ferreira's men then needed penalties to overcome LDU Quito in the quarter-finals and Fluminense in the semi-finals. Goalkeeper Carlos Miguel proved crucial on both occasions, making three saves in total.

After losing the national title to Flamengo last Saturday, Palmeiras fielded a reserve side in Tuesday’s visit to Chapecoense and suffered a 3-0 defeat.

Although the result did not change their position in the Brasileiro table, Palmeiras are now winless in four matches across all competitions. They have also conceded in each of their last five outings.

Like Palmeiras, Estudiantes have also faced the same opponent four times in this edition: Flamengo, the reigning continental champions and two-time Brazilian champions.

In Group A, Alexander Medina's men suffered a narrow defeat at the Maracana and drew 1-1 at the Jorge Luis Hirschi. In the semi-finals, the Pincha held the favourites to two goalless draws before goalkeeper Fernando Muslera starred in the shootout, saving penalties from Jorginho, Lucas Paqueta, and Bruno Henrique.

That trademark Argentine resilience was also evident against Universidad Catolica in Chile, and especially across the two quarter-final matches against Corinthians.

Estudiantes have conceded an average of just 0.5 goals per match across their last 10 Libertadores games. Since the round of 16, Muslera has been beaten only twice.

Their main concern is at the other end: Estudiantes have scored no more than once in nine of their last 10 matches in the tournament. A closely fought contest in Montevideo could therefore be in prospect.

According to recent reports, palmeiras’ medical staff are racing to get defender Murilo fit after he sustained a left-thigh injury. If he is unavailable, Bruno Fuchs is expected to join captain Gustavo Gomez and Alexander Barboza in the back three, ahead of youngster Luis Benedetti.

According to recent reports, forward Paulinho is also a major doubt after developing inflammation in the muscle and bone tissue in his calf. Even if he recovers, he could miss the Copa do Brasil final.

Uruguay international full-back Joaquin Piquerez was rested against Rubro-Negro but is expected to return on the left in his home country.

Fellow full-back Jefte remains provisionally suspended pending a hearing before the Anti-Doping Sports Justice Tribunal (TJD-AD).

For Estudiantes, former Sao Paulo midfielder Gabriel Neves is still recovering from a fractured arm and is likely to miss out.

Neves joins midfielder Baltasar Rodriguez, who is suspended after being sent off in the second leg of the semi-final.

Joaquin Correa sustained a grade-two muscle injury to his right thigh against Talleres on November 7.

With the usual recovery period around three weeks, the former Botafogo forward is undergoing intensive treatment in a bid to make the bench.

Palmeiras possible starting lineup:.

Miguel; Gomez, Murilo, Barboza; Giay, Freitas, Pereira, Piquerez; Arias, Roque, Lopez.

Estudiantes possible starting lineup:.

Muslera; Mancuso, Nunez, Palacios, Rojo; Piovi, Burgos, Castro, Palacios, Cetre; Carrillo.

With two solid, well-organised defences and goalkeepers in good form, a high-scoring contest seems unlikely.

Palmeiras may dominate possession, but Estudiantes could respond with a set-piece goal if they fall behind.

If the final goes to penalties, Muslera could have the chance to redeem himself after a difficult World Cup.

#153705. Rare-variant genetic architecture of height in over 1.4 million individuals

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 80m • 📚 Deep Dive (15906 w)
📖 Baca

Rare-variant genetic architecture of height in over 1.4 million individuals

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 80 min read (15906 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~80 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Highly heritable, polygenic and easily measured, adult height has long been the model trait in human genetics1,2.
  • Although height was described as a heritable trait as early as 18863, its genetic architecture started to emerge only in the late twentieth century when researchers began identifying the genetic causes of Mendelian syndromes with a substantial stature component4,5,6,7.
  • In a recent development, by contrast, sequencing-based studies of rare variation can directly implicate causal genes by identifying large-effect putative loss-of-function (pLoF) and missense variants9.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Highly heritable, polygenic and easily measured, adult height has long been the model trait in human genetics1,2. Although the landscape of height-associated common genetic variation has been studied extensively2, rare variation remains relatively unexplored1. Here, using rare protein-altering variants in a discovery set of 826,066 exomes, we identify 207 height-associated genes, 98% of which replicate in an additional 624,567 individuals. The rarest and most deleterious class of variation, singleton (frequency < 0.0001%) putative loss-of-function variants, implicated 17 genes with large effects on height ranging from −17cm (ACAN) to +11 cm (FBN1) per allele, 52× larger than the average effect of common height-associated variants and comparable to the 1% tails of a common variant polygenic score. Several genes (TET1, DTL and IGF2BP2) have effect sizes that are at least as large as established Mendelian height genes, yet lack documented stature or skeletal growth syndromes, particularly for genes associated with increased height. Our large-scale sequencing study elucidates the genetic architecture and allelic heterogeneity of rare variants in height, providing unique insights into their large effects—often similar to or larger than recognized Mendelian syndromes—and their impact on trait prediction, clinical evaluation, and discovery power to facilitate drug target prioritization.

Although height was described as a heritable trait as early as 18863, its genetic architecture started to emerge only in the late twentieth century when researchers began identifying the genetic causes of Mendelian syndromes with a substantial stature component4,5,6,7. Non-syndromic genetic modulators of height remained unclear until 2007, when genome-wide association studies (GWASs) identified the first common variants associated with height8. Fifteen years later, a GWAS of 5.3 million individuals identified 12,111 independent variants that collectively accounted for 40% of the variance in height across individuals of European descent2. As with other traits, height GWASs predominantly implicated common non-coding variants with modest effects (<1 cm)2, complicating efforts to link associations directly to specific genes and functional mechanisms.

In a recent development, by contrast, sequencing-based studies of rare variation can directly implicate causal genes by identifying large-effect putative loss-of-function (pLoF) and missense variants9. To systematically assess the contribution of rare coding variation to height, we performed a multiancestry exome sequencing analysis of adult height in 1,450,633 individuals across 12 cohorts (Supplementary Table 1), in which we (1) identified 17 height-associated genes through a burden of singleton pLoFs; (2) identified additional height-associated genes by including nonsynonymous variants up to 1% alternate allele frequency (AAF) and applying non-burden tests that do not assume variant effects act in the same direction; and (3) estimated the impact of rare protein-altering variation on genetic-based height prediction.

In a recent development, using 826,066 individuals from six cohorts (Supplementary Table 1), we performed three discovery association analyses of adult height: (1) imputed common variants (AAF > 0.01); (2) rare exome variants (AAF ≤ 0.01, alternate allele count (AAC) ≥ 10); and (3) gene-based tests grouping rare coding variants. We used a single unified Bonferroni significance threshold of 1.75 × 10−9 across all three analyses (Methods). For gene-based analyses, we used a gene-wide omnibus statistic, gene-P10, that aggregates evidence across burden tests and two other gene-based tests, variant-level aggregate Cauchy association tests (ACAT-V)11 and optimal sequence kernel association tests (SKAT-O)12 (Methods and Supplementary Fig. 1). We used six additional cohorts with 624,567 individuals for replication (Supplementary Table 1) and assessed the impact of rare variants on height prediction using a subset (n = 242,679).

Common variant analysis identified 3,034 conditionally independent height associations (Supplementary Table 2) that collectively explain around 25% of the observed variation in height (Methods and Supplementary Note). We conditioned on these 3,034 common variants to ensure rare variant and gene-based associations were independent of common variant signals (Supplementary Note and Supplementary Fig. 2). We identified 105 rare nonsynonymous variants in 87 genes (median AAF = 2.16 × 10−3; Supplementary Table 3) and 207 genes associated with height (gene-P < 1.75 × 10−9; Extended Data Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 4). In total, 82 out of the 87 genes with significant rare nonsynonymous variant associations are also among the 207 genes identified through gene-based tests.

Industry observers note that as singleton pLoFs represent the rarest and most deleterious class of variants, we first focused on this subset. Singleton pLoF burden tests identified 17 genes, 11 height decreasing and 6 height increasing, with a mean absolute effect of 8.92 cm per allele (Fig. 1, Table 1 and Supplementary Tables 5 and 6), about 52× larger than the average GWAS variant (\(\overline{|{\beta }_{\mathrm{GWAS}}|}\) = 0.17 cm) and around 44× larger (range 14.4× to 78.3×) when comparing effects per gene (Methods and Supplementary Table 7). Effects ranged from a 16.6-cm decrease in stature for ACAN singleton pLoF carriers to an 11.1-cm increase in stature for FBN1 singleton pLoF carriers. The effect of carrying a singleton pLoF in one of these 17 genes approaches the cumulative effect observed in the 1% tails of a common variant polygenic score (PGS) (top 1%, +9.60 cm; bottom 1%, −9.12 cm; Fig. 2a, Methods and Supplementary Tables 8 and 9). These incredibly rare pLoFs, cumulatively carried by fewer than 0.1% of individuals (744 carriers among 826,066 individuals), have a larger impact on height than all but the most extreme combinations of common variants.

In a recent development, a, pLoF burden effect sizes across AAFs for 17 genes identified by a significant burden of singleton pLoFs (Table 1). b, Same genes as in a, with effect sizes from singleton burden tests across variant classes displayed. c, The relationship between AAF, variant class, effect size, and discovery yield for 179 genes identified from burden tests (Supplementary Tables 6 and 10). Inside each point is the number of genes discovered (top) and the absolute mean effect (in centimetres; bottom). Effect sizes were estimated by multiplying β by the s.d. of observed height (about 7.99 cm). All P values are two-sided, calculated by REGENIE in discovery analysis (n = 826,066), and significance assessed using a P-value threshold of 1.75 × 10−9.

a, Percentiles of a height PGS (grey) derived from common variants (AAF > 1%; 3,034 GWAS variants + 5 common exome variants; Supplementary Table 8) representing the mean height difference between replication individuals in each PGS percentile (n = 2,427) compared with the remaining ancestry/sex-matched individuals (n = 240,252; Supplementary Table 9). The coloured points are mean significant burden test effect sizes (split by effect direction) placed for comparison to the PGS. The error bars represent 95% CIs around the mean effect estimated from REGENIE. b, The inverse relationship between effect size (in centimetres; y axis) and AAF (x axis) for burden tests (Supplementary Table 6), exome variants (Supplementary Table 3) and conditionally independent common variants (Supplementary Table 2) from discovery (n = 826,066 individuals). The triangles denote burden tests (with a smaller shape for the burden AAF threshold embedded inside), and the circles denote individual variants. The colour denotes the predicted consequence of individual variants or variants included in the burden test. The full distribution is shown in the inset.

These 17 genes belong to well-established biological processes and pathways affecting height, including extracellular matrix organization and skeletal/growth pathways such as growth hormone/insulin-like growth factor (GH/IGF), WNT/β-catenin and transforming growth factor-β1,13,14,15 (TGFβ) (Table 1 and Extended Data Table 1).

Incorporating more common variation into burden tests can increase statistical power for gene discovery by adding variant carriers, although at the cost of attenuated effect sizes. Expanding our analysis to include increasingly frequent pLoFs, followed by including missense variants, identified an additional 162 genes (Extended Data Fig. 1).

Among pLoFs, relaxing the burden test AAF threshold from singletons (about 0.00006%) to 1% identified 76 genes, 62 not discovered with pLoF singletons alone. On average, burden tests aggregating more common pLoFs had a 3.96-cm effect—less than half the 8.92-cm effect of pLoF singletons, but still 24× larger than the average GWAS association (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Table 10). Among the 15 genes with pLoF singleton associations that remained significant at AAF < 0.01%, we observed a 35% attenuation in the absolute effect size (from 8.71 cm to 5.68 cm), suggesting that a substantial fraction of more frequent pLoF-annotated variants may not cause complete loss of function. Two genes—CHD8 (associated with autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability) and COL1A1 (associated with Ehlers–Danlos syndrome16 and osteogenesis imperfecta)—were identified only through singleton pLoF burden tests. When more frequent pLoFs were included, burden test effect sizes fell by 78% for COL1A1 and 83% for CHD8 and were no longer statistically significant (Fig. 1a). By contrast, three genes with absolute effects on height of >1 s.d. (7.99 cm) reached significance only with higher-frequency pLoFs: SHOX17 in the fibroblast growth factor pathway (β = −12.05 cm, P = 2.85 × 10−16); transcriptional regulator ERF (β = −8.67 cm, P = 4.41 × 10−21); and HMGA2, the insulin-like growth factor pathway gene underlying the first height GWAS discovery8 (β = −8.11 cm, P = 6.11 × 10−13). These three genes each had few singleton pLoFs (1, 6, and 16 carriers, respectively); aggregating singletons with additional rare pLoFs was therefore essential to achieve significance.

This expanded set of height-associated pLoF burden genes highlighted additional canonical growth pathways and height biology (for example, the fibroblast growth factor pathway; Extended Data Table 1), as well as additional members from the same gene families and pathways implicated by pLoF singleton genes (Supplementary Table 11).

Whereas pLoFs represent the rarest and most deleterious class of coding variation, missense variants represent the most frequent class of protein-altering variants9,18,19. If missense variants ablate protein function to a similar extent as pLoFs, we might expect both increased statistical power and similar effect sizes when combining both in burden tests. Conversely, if missense variants only partially diminish protein function or exert opposing effects through gain-of-function (GoF) mechanisms, burden effect sizes will be attenuated.

We combined pLoFs with three sets of missense variants: (1) all missense variants; (2) missense variants inconsistently classified as deleterious by in silico algorithms (possibly deleterious); and (3) missense variants confidently classified as deleterious by in silico algorithms (deleterious; Methods), collectively identifying 154 genes (85 not discovered by pLoFs alone; Fig. 1c). When combined with pLoF variants, successively filtering rare missense variants for increasing deleteriousness increased discovery power, yielding 96, 116, and 132 genes for each of the above groups, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 1b).

Among the 14 genes with both significant singleton pLoF and singleton pLoF + deleterious missense burden associations (Table 1), the absolute effect size decreased 28.5% on average when adding deleterious missense singletons (8.70 cm versus 6.22 cm; Fig. 1b). This observation holds broadly across height-associated genes, with diminished pLoF + missense effect sizes reflecting both that missense variants account for most rare allele carriers (68.5% in singleton and 84.1% in AAF < 1% burden tests) and that the effect of missense variants is, on average, substantially smaller than that of pLoFs (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Table 10). Despite diminished effect sizes, the higher allele counts contributed by missense variants substantially increased overall discovery power, more than doubling the number of associated height genes.

Of the 85 genes not discovered by pLoFs alone, UHRF2 (singleton pLoF + deleterious missense variants: β = −4.74 cm, P = 3.6 × 10−12)—an E3 ubiquitin ligase regulating the cell cycle20—and PTPN11 (pLoF + deleterious missense variants AAF < 0.01%: β = −4.00 cm, P = 2.5 × 10−32)—a signalling protein involved in development and hormone response through the RAS–MAPK and PI3K–AKT signalling pathways21—had the largest effect sizes.

According to recent reports, we found six genes (ESR1, FGFR3, HSD11B2, MTMR11, PTPN11 and RPL5) that exhibited the strongest association from missense-only burden tests, and pLoF burden tests were, at best, only nominally significant (Supplementary Table 13). Four genes (FGFR3, HSD11B2, PTPN11 and RPL5) had opposite directions of effect between pLoF and missense burden tests, although the pLoF estimates were not statistically significant. Notably, three genes—FGFR3 (refs. 7,22), PTPN11 (ref. 23) and ESR1 (ref. 24)—have previously reported GoF mutations that drive syndromic conditions with notable skeletal growth phenotypes, including achondroplasia (FGFR3)22 and Noonan syndrome (PTPN11)23. Given the known GoF mechanisms for three of these genes, the other missense-driven genes may also affect height through GoF mechanisms.

The latest genes identified by incorporating missense variants further underscore previously implicated pathways, biological functions and gene families (Supplementary Table 11) but also implicate different pathways (for example, Sonic Hedgehog signalling) and biological processes, including sex hormone regulation and carbohydrate transport, storage and metabolism (Extended Data Table 1).

Sources indicate that although burden tests identified 179 height-associated genes (Extended Data Fig. 1a), they were not designed to identify genes of which variants with effects exist in opposite directions or where most variants have no effect. For these situations, SKAT-O12 and ACAT-V11 were developed.

It has been revealed that collectively, ACAT-V and SKAT-O identified 28 genes not detected by burden tests (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Before conditional analysis, ACAT-V and SKAT-O associations were more likely than burden test associations to be driven by linkage disequilibrium with common variants (Supplementary Note, Supplementary Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 12). Consistent with the underlying model, SKAT-O associations highlight genes harbouring variants with opposing effects on height. For example, in PTCH1, a transmembrane protein receptor involved in Hedgehog signalling25, the SKAT-O association (P = 1.94 × 10−15) was driven by two variants: a missense variant associated with increased height (9:95458026G>A; p.T1052M; β = +1.00 cm, P = 4.8 × 10−11; Supplementary Table 3) and a splice acceptor variant associated with decreased height (9:95485875C>T; β = −4.28 cm, P = 1.9 × 10−9). Meanwhile, ACAT-V identified genes like FBN2 (P = 1.72 × 10−12), a component of microfibrils that stores and regulates growth factors including TGFβ26, in which the association was driven by one significant missense variant (5:128332993G>T; p.H1381N; β = +1.07 cm, P = 9.8 × 10−14; AAF = 0.48%; Supplementary Table 3).

Although gene-based tests are useful for boosting rare variant discovery power, we identified 121 significant rare (AAF < 1%) exome variants after conditioning on common GWAS variants (Fig. 2b, Supplementary Tables 3 and 14 and Supplementary Note). Of these 121 variants, 105 were nonsynonymous (85 missense, 17 pLoFs and 3 in-frame insertions or deletions (indels)) and implicated 87 genes, 82 of which overlapped genes implicated by gene-based tests (60 from burden tests; 22 genes from ACAT-V or SKAT-O).

According to recent reports, for the 82 genes identified by both single variants and gene-based tests, we compared the consistency of effect sizes between burden test and significant individual variants (Methods). Focusing on the 79 rare nonsynonymous variants (59 missense, 17 pLoFs, 3 in-frame indels) in 60 genes with a significant burden test, we found that 52 (66%) had larger effect sizes than the largest burden test effect. The neurodevelopmental-disorder-associated gene KMT2B27 had the largest discrepancy, with a nearly 20-fold difference between variant 19:35720959C>T (p.R538C; β = −7.67 cm, P = 2.6 × 10−10, AAF = 2.61 × 10−5) and the largest burden test effect (β = −0.38 cm, P = 5.0×10−10; pLoF and possibly deleterious missense variants with AAF < 0.01%).

Two genes with GoF missense variants, FGFR3 and PTPN11, have multiple missense variants with some of the largest observed effects on height (Fig. 2b). Among the six exome-wide significant variants in FGFR3, a pathogenic GoF missense variant causing achondroplasia7 (4:1804392G>A; p.G380R; P = 3.22 × 10−64) decreases height by 29.78 cm, about 13× larger than the largest FGFR3 burden test effect (β = −2.31 cm, P = 2 × 10−41; deleterious missense variants AAF < 0.0001; Extended Data Fig. 2). PTPN11 also contains two significant pathogenic GoF missense variants23,28: p.R265Q (12:112472981G>A; β = −12.26 cm, P = 6 × 10−19) and p.N308D (12:112477719A>G; β = −14.21 cm, P = 4 × 10−14), with effects around 3× larger than the largest burden signal (β = −4.12 cm, P = 3.6 × 10−33; deleterious missense variants with AAF < 0.0001). These examples emphasize the challenge that allelic heterogeneity presents for interpreting and using gene-level burden effect sizes. We discuss the implications of effect size heterogeneity on phenotypic prediction below (see the ‘Heritability, enrichment and prediction’ section).

Recent findings suggest that recent studies29,30 demonstrated that non-additive models can identify associations missed by standard approaches; we therefore tested rare coding variants under a recessive model. This identified only one association missed by additive tests: the CFTR ΔF508 mutation that causes cystic fibrosis31 was not associated with height under an additive model (βadd = −0.05 cm; Padd = 0.14), but was associated with a 5.87-cm height reduction in homozygotes in the recessive model (Prec = 5 × 10−10; replication and additional details are provided in the Supplementary Note). This result is consistent with both the recessive nature of cystic fibrosis mutations and the established impact of cystic fibrosis on growth and stature. The inability of cystic fibrosis treatments to fully restore growth trajectory and stature, along with diminished IGF1 levels exhibited by newborns with cystic fibrosis, are findings compatible with a direct effect of CFTR on height through fetal and/or neonatal growth pathways32,33.

We sought to understand the differences in genetic architecture across genetic ancestry groups by stratifying single-variant and gene-based tests by ancestry (Methods). Consistent with previous findings, we detected no effect-size heterogeneity by genetic ancestry34. However, we identified several ancestry-specific signals resulting from differences in AAF and sample size. Most associations specific to a single ancestry were identified in the European subset, which accounts for most participants (n = 640,240, 78%; Supplementary Table 15 and Supplementary Note). One notable exception is a rare HHIP p.V496E substitution associated with decreased height exclusively in the admixed American subpopulation (AMR AAF = 0.05%, P = 1.52 × 10−9, β = −3.96 cm; Supplementary Table 15 and Supplementary Note). This variant is observed only in individuals from the Mexico City Prospective Study35. We speculate that the p.V496E variant is a GoF missense variant, as rare HHIP pLoFs appear to be associated with increased height (pLoF singleton β = +9.92 cm, P = 3.72 × 10−7). Similarly, we replicate a known signal at a FBN1 missense variant36 (p.E1297G; β = −2.12 cm, P = 2.9 × 10−17; Supplementary Table 16) that is substantially more common in admixed Americans (about 1% versus 0.004% in Europeans) and occurs almost exclusively on Indigenous haplotypes (Supplementary Fig. 4). These discoveries underscore the value of sequencing diverse populations.

According to recent reports, height GWASs14 have consistently observed enrichment of Mendelian syndrome genes among height-associated common variant loci37; we observed similar enrichment in genes implicated through rare variation. Forty-three out of 76 genes (57%) with significant pLoF burden signals at AAF < 1% and 102 out of 207 (49%) height-associated genes in total were documented in the Mendelian syndrome in Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM) database, significantly more than expected by chance (odds ratio (OR) = 4.46, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 2.76–7.26, P = 1.83 × 10−10; Fisher’s exact test). Of the 43 Mendelian genes, 21 had annotated stature or skeletal growth features2, an 8.37-fold enrichment (95% CI = 4.34–16.10, P = 2.56 × 10−10; Fisher’s exact test). Genes with pLoF burden height associations and a Mendelian syndrome listed in OMIM are over 5× more likely to be associated with decreased height (36 out of 43, 83%). Among the 11 pLoF singleton genes with height-decreasing effects, 9 were in OMIM and 8 list stature or skeletal growth among the clinical characteristics. By contrast, among the six with height-increasing effects, three are in OMIM, but only FBN1 includes height among the clinical characteristics. Our results were insufficient to determine whether increased height is under-reported as a syndromic feature or whether genes leading to increased height are less likely to cause other clinical features and therefore cause fewer recognized syndromes (Supplementary Note).

Industry observers note that previous studies estimated that the gene nearest to a GWAS peak is the causal gene in around 70% of instances9,38. We observed strong overlap between large-effect rare variant burden associations and GWAS peaks, although this overlap diminishes noticeably with the stringency of the burden definition and variant frequency. Of pLoF singleton genes, 82% (14 out of 17) are the closest gene to a GWAS peak, compared with only 60% (92 out of 154) of pLoF + missense burden genes. In total, 28 out of 207 genes are not among the top 10 nearest genes to any common variant signal. Notably, 4 genes are >1 Mb from the nearest common variant association signal: FIBIN, HHIPL1, PTPN11 and WLS. Even compared with the 12,111 index variants from ref. 2, PTPN11 is not among the 10 nearest genes to any GWAS peak, with the closest signal 393 kb away (Supplementary Table 4).

To assess the validity of our results, we performed replication analyses in six independent cohorts comprising an additional 624,567 individuals (Supplementary Table 1). Despite the 24.4% smaller sample size, 203 out of 207 (98.1%) genes and 113 out of 125 (90.4%) single variants replicated with nominal significance (α = 0.05; Methods, Supplementary Fig. 5, Supplementary Tables 3 and 4 and Supplementary Note), demonstrating both high consistency of height associations and the robustness of our Bonferroni threshold. Furthermore, replication rates were consistent across gene-based tests—BURDEN-ACAT, 98.1% (155 out of 158); SBAT, 93.8% (166 out of 177); SKAT-O, 95.3% (164 out of 172); and ACAT-V, 94.9% (94 out of 99; Supplementary Fig. 5b–e). Replication performance for single variants improved to 96.1% (98 out of 102) after restricting to variants with over 80% estimated replication power (Supplementary Fig. 5f). Irrespective of power, all 179 burden genes and all but one variant had consistent directions of effect between discovery and replication analyses (Supplementary Note). Furthermore, gene-based tests maintained high replication rates well above our study-wide P-value threshold (Supplementary Note and Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6). For example, 91.6% of the 368 genes reaching a discovery gene-P < 2.5 × 10−6—roughly equivalent to one test per gene—replicated with nominal significance (P < 0.05) and would implicate an additional 137 genes compared to our experiment-wide Bonferroni threshold (Supplementary Fig. 5a). Replication rates for single variants and singleton burden tests declined similarly, requiring respective P-value thresholds of 4 × 10−6 and 1 × 10−6 to achieve a comparable 91.6% replication rate when restricted to tests with over 80% power (Supplementary Figs. 5f and 6).

Finally, because burden tests were more likely to have negative (height-decreasing) effect estimates, we compared the ratio of effect directions across significance thresholds (Supplementary Note and Extended Data Fig. 3). The excess of height-decreasing burden effects persists well below the Bonferroni significance threshold, with the degree of imbalance varying by both significance threshold and variant class. These patterns suggest considerable rare variant signal yet to be discovered.

Rare variants are frequently offered as an answer to the ‘missing heritability’ problem in complex trait genetics39. Here we estimated the cumulative impact of rare coding variation on height at the population level by calculating the proportion of phenotypic variance attributable to burdens of rare coding variants and assessing the potential of large-effect height-associated coding variants to improve height predictions.

According to recent reports, first, burden heritability regression40 estimated the burden of rare nonsynonymous variants explain 3.97% (95% CI = 3.77–4.17%) of phenotypic variance (Extended Data Fig. 4, Supplementary Table 17 and Supplementary Note), nearly identical to the previously published estimate of 3.82% (95% CI = 3.55–4.09%)40. pLoFs with AAF < 0.001% accounted for the largest fraction of burden heritability, consistent with the large effects we observed for these extremely rare, damaging variants. This probably underestimates the true contribution of rare coding variants because the burden approach underestimates heritability in the presence of effect size heterogeneity40. Together, the most significant burden test for each of the 179 burden genes explains around 1.1% of phenotypic variance in the replication data, nearly 30% of the total estimated contribution of the burden of rare variants to adult height (Extended Data Fig. 5).

Sources indicate that we next tested for enrichment of rare, deleterious variants in individuals whose height was poorly predicted by common variants in our replication data (n = 242,679), as rare variants unaccounted for in common variant prediction may contribute to the discrepancy between observed and genetically predicted height41,42,43. Individuals deviating from their common variant predicted height by >2.5 s.d. (±17–20 cm) were 17.2-fold (95% CI = 9.89–28.34, P = 1.12 × 10−16, Fisher’s exact test) enriched for carrying a singleton pLoF in one of the 17 singleton pLoF genes (Fig. 3a, Methods and Supplementary Table 18). By contrast, individuals at the extreme ends of the height distribution (>2.5 s.d.) were only 4.9-fold enriched (P = 1.89 × 10−7, Fisher’s exact test; Supplementary Table 19 and Supplementary Note) for pLoF singletons in these genes, consistent with previous results42,43.

In a recent development, we next focused on the 337 individuals in the replication data carrying a pLoF singleton in one of the 17 genes with significant pLoF singleton burden (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 5). In these individuals, adding burden effects to a common variant prediction model (Methods) improved the R2 from 0.55 to 0.72 (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Note). This brings the performance in line with common variant prediction across the entire replication sample (R2 = 0.73). Including pLoF singleton burden effects into prediction also reduced the s.d. of the error distribution by 1.55 cm, signifying more consistent predictions; however, improvement varied substantially by gene (Fig. 3c,d and Extended Data Fig. 6).

Given the large effects of rare missense variants in FGFR3 and PTPN11 (Fig. 2b), we evaluated the performance of several rare variant-based prediction models compared with standard common variant PGS in these variant carriers (Fig. 3d and Methods). Among 29 carriers of five rare deleterious missense variants in these two genes in the replication dataset, the prediction R2 dropped slightly from 0.158 to 0.155 when adding a PGS built from deleterious missense (AAF < 1%) burden effect sizes (Supplementary Fig. 7). By contrast, the prediction R2 increased to 0.67 when adding a PGS based on individually significant rare variants. This difference in prediction performance was especially pronounced among the six carriers of FGFR3 p.G380R (4:1804392:G:A; βdiscovery = −29.8 cm, P = 3.2 × 10−64; Fig. 2b)—a ClinVar pathogenic variant reported for achondroplasia7 (Fig. 3d))—for whom height prediction improved by an average of 26.1 cm after accounting for the variant. Aggregate burden effects are largely unsuitable in prediction for genes with substantial effect size heterogeneity, such as FGFR3 and PTPN11 (Supplementary Note). Still, individual rare variants are difficult to incorporate in prediction, as variants are frequently not observed in reference samples or effects are estimated from few observations. Overall, we observe that PGSs that supplement common variants with both aggregate rare variant effects and individual rare variants with extreme effects perform best for height prediction (Supplementary Fig. 8).

Sources indicate that finally, population-based data can provide a useful orthogonal resource to aid clinical variant interpretation19. We assessed whether our association results could inform pathogenicity classification of ClinVar variants with conflicting classifications of pathogenicity (CCOPs) or variants of uncertain significance (VUSs). To maximize power for these ultrarare variants, we performed a meta-analysis of our discovery and replication data (Supplementary Tables 20 and 21 and Extended Data Fig. 7) for the 5,233 rare variants in our 207 height-associated genes that were evaluated in ClinVar for links to stature-related syndromes (Methods). In total, 39 variants were significantly associated with height, including 20 VUSs/CCOPs. Of those 20 variants, one—an ADAMTS10 splice region variant—was associated with increased height (β = +2.3 cm, P = 3.9 × 10−15), the opposite direction of ADAMTS10’s burden test effects (Supplementary Table 6). The pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) category contained more significant height-associated variants than expected by chance (P = 6 × 10−12, binomial test), as did the CCOP and benign/likely benign categories (Supplementary Table 22).

Industry observers note that we next looked for variants absent from ClinVar with absolute effect sizes greater than 7.99 cm (1 s.d.), an effect size greater than 77% of the stature-related P/LP variants in our 207 genes (Fig. 4). At this effect size threshold, four significant variants were completely absent from ClinVar as of July 2025 (Supplementary Table 21): pLoFs in HMGA2 (p.E98*), LCORL (p.S1370Rfs*10) and ADAMTS17 (p.S971*), and a missense substitution in ZFAT (p.R762C).
